How you'll be evaluated
Goal clarity · Metric selection · Trade-offs and guardrails · Measurement plan

title: Conversion in community moderation declined after a pricing or policy change. Diagnose it
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager for a community moderation product used by content moderators, community admins, and Trust & Safety operations teams to review reported content, act on policy violations, and keep user communities safe. Shortly after a pricing or policy change, the team sees a significant decline in conversion within the moderation workflow.

The change may have affected eligibility, feature access, moderator incentives, enforcement rules, queue prioritization, or the cost of using moderation capabilities. The decline is concerning because lower conversion could mean fewer communities adopting moderation tools, fewer flagged items receiving action, slower enforcement, or reduced moderator confidence in the system.

Your task is to diagnose the decline as an RCA problem. You should frame the anomaly clearly, define what “conversion” means in this moderation context, identify where the drop is happening, and determine whether the issue is caused by user behavior, product experience, policy interpretation, pricing impact, operational workflow changes, or measurement errors.

Your diagnosis should consider:
- The exact conversion metric, denominator, funnel steps, and time window before vs. after the pricing or policy change
- Segmentation by moderator type, community size, geography, content category, platform, enforcement policy, and paid vs. free eligibility
- Instrumentation checks, event tracking changes, data pipeline issues, and whether the metric definition changed during rollout
- Differences between adoption decline, workflow completion decline, action-rate decline, and appeal/reversal-rate changes
- Potential moderator pain points such as unclear policy guidance, reduced access to tools, higher cost, more friction, or lower trust in recommendations
- Evidence needed from logs, funnel analytics, moderator feedback, support tickets, QA audits, and safety outcome metrics
- Short-term mitigation options, longer-term prevention mechanisms, and how to monitor whether safety outcomes are recovering

The goal is to demonstrate a structured RCA approach that separates correlation from causation, protects community safety while the issue is investigated, and helps the team make a confident decision on whether to fix, roll back, iterate, or further monitor the pricing or policy change.

title: Define success metrics for creator sponsorship marketplace serving first-time buyers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a creator sponsorship marketplace where brands or agencies that have never purchased a sponsorship before are trying to find creators, send outreach, negotiate terms, and get enough confidence to launch their first campaign. The business goal is to improve response time in this marketplace, especially for first-time buyers who may be unfamiliar with creator norms, pricing, messaging quality, and expected turnaround.

In this interview, define the success metrics you would use to evaluate whether the marketplace is performing well for these first-time buyers. Your answer should clarify what “response time” means in the context of the buyer and creator workflow, how it should be measured, and how it connects to buyer trust, marketplace liquidity, and eventual campaign success.

Focus on building a metrics framework that is useful for product decisions, not just reporting. Consider where response delays may occur, which users or transactions should be included or excluded, how to avoid misleading averages, and how to detect whether faster responses are improving the buyer experience without degrading creator quality or marketplace health.

The experience should consider:

- The end-to-end workflow from buyer signup, creator discovery, outreach, creator reply, negotiation, booking, and campaign launch.
- A precise definition of the response-time metric, including start event, end event, denominator, and handling of no-response cases.
- Segmentation for first-time buyers, creator types, campaign categories, budget ranges, geographies, and outreach channels.
- Instrumentation needed to capture buyer messages, creator replies, timestamps, availability, automated responses, and status changes reliably.
- Cohorts that distinguish new buyers from returning buyers, new creators from experienced creators, and marketplace supply-constrained segments.
- Guardrail metrics for response quality, booking conversion, buyer satisfaction, creator burden, spammy outreach, cancellations, and long-term retention.
- Decision usefulness: how the metrics would help diagnose whether delays come from buyer behavior, creator responsiveness, product friction, pricing mismatch, or marketplace liquidity.
- Edge cases such as bulk outreach, off-platform communication, bot or templated replies, time zones, weekends, and creators who are unavailable.

The goal is to define a clear, actionable metrics system that helps the product team understand whether the marketplace is reducing response-time friction for first-time buyers while preserving a healthy, trusted sponsorship marketplace for both buyers and creators.

title: Choose north star and guardrail metrics for a new privacy controls
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a newly launched privacy controls experience for administrators of a large-scale digital product. These administrators may manage privacy settings for an organization, team, family, merchant account, developer workspace, or regulated customer environment, and they need confidence that sensitive data usage, sharing, retention, consent, and access preferences are configured correctly.

The product team wants to know whether the new controls are improving trust without creating confusion, unnecessary friction, or unsafe misconfiguration. Your task is to define a north star metric and supporting guardrail metrics that would help the team understand whether the experience is successful after launch.

Focus on metrics that are specific, measurable, and useful for product decisions. Be clear about what each metric measures, who is included in the denominator, how the event or state would be instrumented, and how you would interpret changes across administrator cohorts or customer segments.

The experience should consider:
- The administrator workflow from discovering privacy controls to reviewing, changing, saving, and auditing settings
- How to define the eligible population and denominator for privacy-control usage
- Whether success should reflect adoption, correct configuration, confidence, reduction in risk, or ongoing engagement
- Instrumentation needed to distinguish views, edits, confirmations, reversions, errors, and support-seeking behavior
- Cohorts such as new vs. existing administrators, organization size, regulated vs. non-regulated customers, and permission level
- Guardrails for user confusion, accidental lockouts, degraded product usage, compliance risk, support burden, or trust erosion
- How the metrics would guide decisions on launch readiness, iteration, education, defaults, and alerting

Your goal is to propose a concise metrics framework that helps the team judge whether the privacy controls are creating administrator trust and safer privacy management, while ensuring that the product does not introduce harmful friction, misleading signals, or operational risk.

title: Prioritize the roadmap for rental home search and verification when engineering capacity is cut in half under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the PM for a real estate rental marketplace focused on helping relocating renters find trustworthy homes in unfamiliar cities. The product includes rental search, listing detail pages, broker/landlord contact flows, listing verification, locality information, and lead qualification. The business depends on generating high-quality property leads while maintaining renter trust and marketplace supply.

Your roadmap was originally planned around improving search relevance, expanding verified listings, reducing fraudulent or stale inventory, improving broker response quality, and adding richer neighborhood decision support. Mid-cycle, engineering capacity is cut in half, while user demand is growing across markets and regulatory scrutiny around listing accuracy, privacy, accessibility, and fair housing practices is increasing.

You need to decide what to prioritize, defer, simplify, or stop. The execution challenge is not just ranking features; it is building a practical operating plan that balances renter trust, broker incentives, verification cost, data freshness, compliance risk, and near-term lead outcomes under constrained engineering and operational bandwidth.

The experience should consider:
- The end-to-end workflow for relocating renters: search, shortlist, verify trust signals, contact property representatives, schedule visits, and decide whether to pursue a listing.
- The roadmap items competing for scarce capacity, such as search relevance, verified listing coverage, fraud/staleness detection, broker response tooling, lead quality improvements, and locality insights.
- Dependencies across engineering, data science, operations, legal/compliance, customer support, broker partnerships, and marketplace supply teams.
- Sequencing choices, including what must ship now, what can be manual or operationally supported, what can be phased by market, and what should be paused.
- Go/no-go criteria for launches, including lead quality, verification accuracy, renter trust, operational load, regulatory risk, and broker adoption.
- Rollback and mitigation plans if verification signals are wrong, broker incentives create spam, lead volume drops, or support escalations increase.
- Communication plans for internal stakeholders, brokers/landlords, operations teams, and renters when product scope or verification standards change.

Your goal is to describe how you would prioritize and execute the roadmap under these constraints, including the operating model, trade-offs, decision criteria, launch sequencing, risk management, and how you would ensure the reduced roadmap still improves qualified property leads without compromising renter trust or regulatory responsibility.

title: Create a launch plan for cross-border payment setup aimed at freelancers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are launching a cross-border payment setup experience for freelancers who work with international buyers. The product must help freelancers configure how they receive money across currencies and countries, while giving buyers confidence that payments are secure, trackable, compliant, and likely to reach the right recipient without delays or surprises.

This is an execution-focused question. Your task is to create a practical launch plan, not to design every product detail. Assume the product has core payment capabilities available, but the launch must coordinate product readiness, compliance, operations, support, risk controls, communications, and measurement before making it broadly available to freelancers and their buyers.

The launch should account for the trust gap that often exists in cross-border freelance work: buyers may worry about fraud, failed transfers, unclear fees, refund or dispute handling, identity verification, delivery confidence, and lack of visibility once money moves across borders. Freelancers, meanwhile, need a setup flow that is understandable, reliable, and compatible with their local banking or wallet options.

The experience should consider:
- Target launch scope, including initial countries, currencies, freelancer segments, and buyer use cases
- Key owners and workstreams across product, engineering, compliance, risk, finance, support, legal, marketing, and partnerships
- Dependencies such as KYC/KYB checks, bank or payment-rail integrations, FX handling, fraud monitoring, tax or regulatory requirements, and customer support readiness
- Sequencing from internal testing to pilot, limited rollout, broader launch, and post-launch optimization
- Go/no-go criteria tied to payment success, verification completion, fraud rates, support load, buyer trust signals, and operational readiness
- Buyer-facing and freelancer-facing communication needed to explain fees, timing, security, disputes, and payment status
- Rollback or containment plans if transfers fail, compliance issues arise, fraud spikes, or buyer confidence deteriorates
- Launch risks, including regulatory constraints, currency volatility, failed payouts, chargebacks, account takeover, unclear UX, and support escalations

Your goal is to present a launch plan that shows how you would safely bring this cross-border payment setup to market for freelancers while improving buyer confidence. Focus on sequencing, ownership, readiness checks, risk mitigation, and measurable launch outcomes rather than proposing a full product solution.

title: You're a PM for Meta. Design a product for group travel.

Problem framing · User empathy · Prioritized solution · Success metrics

title: Design a family account controls for project managers that improves launch reliability
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are designing family account controls for project managers responsible for launching and operating large-scale account-management features, such as parent/guardian permissions, child account restrictions, shared payment controls, consent flows, age-based access, and regional compliance rules. These launches are high-risk because they affect trust, safety, privacy, and access for multiple related users within the same household.

Today, project managers may struggle to coordinate policy requirements, product configuration, QA coverage, rollout readiness, dependency tracking, and post-launch monitoring across engineering, legal, support, trust & safety, localization, and regional teams. A missed configuration or unclear ownership can lead to launch delays, broken family experiences, compliance gaps, support spikes, or forced rollbacks.

Design a product experience that helps project managers plan, validate, coordinate, and launch family account controls more reliably. Focus on the workflow friction PMs face before, during, and immediately after launch, rather than designing only the end-user parental control interface.

The experience should consider:
- How project managers define launch scope, supported family roles, age bands, regions, platforms, and policy constraints.
- How dependencies across legal, privacy, engineering, design, support, data, and regional teams are tracked and made visible.
- How readiness checks, test coverage, configuration validation, and risk reviews fit into the launch workflow.
- How the system helps PMs detect gaps, conflicts, or incomplete approvals before launch.
- How rollout status, incidents, guardrail metrics, and customer-impact signals are monitored after launch.
- How PMs collaborate with stakeholders, assign owners, escalate blockers, and maintain an audit trail.
- How the experience supports global scale, accessibility, customer trust, and safe handling of sensitive family data.

Your goal is to frame the target users, their launch workflow, key pain points, and the product capabilities needed to improve launch reliability for family account controls without prescribing a single solution too early.

title: You're a PM at a top-up team. How would you launch cash deposits? If one of the main KPIs is down, how would you go about addressing it?
description:

Goal clarity · Metric selection · Trade-offs and guardrails · Measurement plan

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling multi-device handoff flow for power users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a multi-device handoff experience used by power users who frequently move active work across phones, tablets, desktops, browsers, and possibly shared or secondary devices. The product goal is localization success: users in different languages, regions, time zones, formats, and regulatory environments should be able to resume context seamlessly without confusion, data loss, or region-specific failures.

In this interview, focus on the technical product trade-offs involved in scaling the handoff flow globally. Consider what must be preserved during handoff, such as session state, permissions, language preferences, content context, input progress, notifications, and device capabilities, while accounting for latency, reliability, privacy, and platform differences.

You are not expected to design every UI screen or produce a full system architecture. Instead, evaluate the key technical decisions a PM would need to make with engineering, design, data, security, localization, and regional operations teams to support a dependable experience for high-frequency users across markets.

The experience should consider:

- Requirements for what “successful handoff” means across devices, locales, languages, and user workflows.
- APIs, data contracts, and state-sync mechanisms needed to preserve context accurately across platforms.
- Reliability expectations for power users, including offline behavior, conflict handling, latency, retry logic, and degraded states.
- Privacy and security constraints around session transfer, authentication, device trust, consent, and shared-device risk.
- Localization-specific challenges such as translated strings, regional formats, locale-specific content, right-to-left layouts, time zones, currencies, and compliance differences.
- Rollout strategy across platforms and countries, including feature flags, compatibility with older app versions, and phased market launches.
- Observability needs, including instrumentation for handoff attempts, completion rates, locale-specific failures, latency, error types, and user recovery paths.
- Product trade-offs between consistency, speed, implementation complexity, platform-native behavior, and global scalability.

Your goal is to frame the technical trade-offs clearly, identify the most important risks and dependencies, and explain how you would help the team make implementation choices that improve localized handoff success for power users at scale.

title: Create a launch plan for a high-risk Ads Manager feature for teen users
description:
About Meta

Prioritization · Planning and sequencing · Stakeholder alignment · Launch criteria

title: Decide whether to invest in creator sponsorship marketplace for project managers to improve appointment attendance
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether a product team should invest in a creator sponsorship marketplace capability aimed at project managers who coordinate sponsorship campaigns, creator approvals, kickoff calls, content reviews, and stakeholder meetings. A key business problem is poor appointment attendance: creators, sponsors, agencies, and internal project owners may book meetings but fail to attend, causing campaign delays, lower marketplace trust, operational rework, and missed revenue opportunities.

The investment could involve marketplace features, scheduling workflows, reminders, incentives, reputation signals, creator/sponsor matching changes, calendar integrations, or operational tooling. The strategic question is whether this is the right area to fund versus other ways to improve campaign completion, creator liquidity, sponsor ROI, or marketplace growth.

You should make a clear recommendation on whether to invest, not just list pros and cons. Your reasoning should address the market and product opportunity, why appointment attendance matters to the marketplace, what alternatives exist, and what evidence or decision gates would make the investment worthwhile.

The experience should consider:
- The current workflow for project managers managing creator sponsorship appointments, including booking, confirmation, reminders, rescheduling, and follow-up
- The users and stakeholders involved: project managers, creators, sponsors, agencies, account managers, and marketplace operations teams
- The size and severity of the appointment-attendance problem, including impact on campaign delivery, revenue, retention, trust, and operational cost
- Strategic options, such as building marketplace-native scheduling tools, integrating with calendars, improving incentives/penalties, using reputation systems, or addressing upstream matching quality
- The company’s right to win in this space, including marketplace data, existing relationships, workflow ownership, and ability to influence both sides of the market
- Key trade-offs around user trust, creator experience, sponsor expectations, operational complexity, global scale, and potential gaming or unfair penalties
- Risks and decision gates, including adoption risk, measurable attendance lift, incremental revenue, marketplace liquidity effects, and whether the problem is frequent enough to justify investment

Your goal is to frame the investment decision, evaluate the opportunity and alternatives, and make a defensible recommendation with clear assumptions, success criteria, and next steps for validation.

title: Create a launch plan for support ticket summarizer aimed at community managers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are launching a support ticket summarizer for community managers who oversee high-volume user communities and need to respond quickly to issues, escalations, policy questions, bug reports, and user complaints. Today, these managers may spend significant time reading long ticket threads, extracting key facts, identifying urgency, and deciding the next response or routing step.

The product is intended to reduce response time by generating concise, reliable summaries of incoming or ongoing support tickets. The launch plan should account for how community managers work across queues, collaboration tools, escalation paths, and customer-facing communication, while ensuring summaries are accurate enough to support timely action.

This is an execution-focused question. You should define how to take the feature from readiness to rollout, including sequencing, ownership, dependencies, launch risks, measurement, and operational safeguards. Avoid focusing only on product ideation; the emphasis is on how you would launch and manage the rollout successfully.

The experience should consider:
- The target users’ workflow, including queue triage, ticket review, escalation, and response drafting
- Launch phases, such as internal testing, pilot rollout, broader release, and post-launch monitoring
- Key owners and dependencies across product, engineering, AI/ML, support operations, legal/privacy, and training teams
- Go/no-go criteria tied to response time, summary quality, reliability, and user adoption
- Risks such as inaccurate summaries, missing critical context, overreliance on AI, latency, and trust erosion
- Rollback or mitigation plans if summaries degrade support quality or slow down workflows
- Communication, enablement, and training needed for community managers to use the feature confidently
- Success metrics and guardrails that show whether response time improves without harming resolution quality or user trust

Your goal is to present a practical launch plan that gets the summarizer into the hands of community managers safely and effectively, while optimizing for faster responses and maintaining support quality at scale.

title: Estimate infrastructure or support load created by personal finance dashboard
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the operational impact of launching or scaling a personal finance dashboard that helps users view accounts, spending, budgets, bills, credit insights, or financial trends in one place. The interview task is to estimate the infrastructure and/or customer support load this product could create, using clear assumptions and a structured guesstimate approach.

Focus on the real usage workflow: users connect financial accounts, sync transactions, refresh balances, categorize spending, receive alerts, and contact support when data looks wrong, connections fail, transactions are missing, or insights feel inaccurate. Your estimate should account for both technical demand, such as data refreshes, API calls, storage, notifications, and compute, and human support demand, such as tickets, chats, escalations, and agent capacity.

You are not expected to know exact industry numbers. The emphasis is on defining scope, choosing reasonable drivers, making assumptions explicit, and showing how changes in adoption, engagement, sync frequency, error rates, and support contact rates affect the final estimate.

The experience should consider:
- The target population and adoption funnel, including registered users, connected-account users, and monthly active users.
- Core usage frequency, such as dashboard visits, account refreshes, transaction imports, alert generation, and report views.
- The unit of infrastructure load being estimated, such as API calls, sync jobs, storage volume, compute events, notification sends, or peak concurrent usage.
- The unit of support load being estimated, such as monthly tickets, chat sessions, calls, escalations, or required support-agent hours.
- Key behavioral assumptions, including number of linked accounts per user, transactions per account, refresh cadence, and percentage of users who encounter issues.
- Segmentation by user type, geography, financial institution reliability, new versus returning users, and power users versus casual users.
- Sensitivity checks for the largest drivers, especially active user count, sync failure rate, support contact rate, and automation/self-serve resolution rate.
- Sanity checks against operational constraints such as agent productivity, response-time expectations, uptime requirements, data privacy sensitivity, and user trust.

The goal is to produce a defensible estimate that helps a product or operations team understand whether the personal finance dashboard can scale reliably, what capacity may be needed, and which assumptions most influence infrastructure cost and support readiness.

title: Decide whether to invest in loyalty rewards engine for content moderators to improve lead conversion
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a strategic investment in a loyalty rewards engine aimed at content moderators, with the stated business outcome of improving lead conversion. The product context is a scaled digital platform where moderators review user-generated content, support trust and safety workflows, and may influence whether prospective customers, creators, or community operators move from initial interest to qualified or converted leads through timely, reliable, high-quality moderation outcomes.

The decision is not simply whether rewards can motivate activity. You need to assess whether a rewards engine is the right lever for the conversion problem versus alternatives such as workflow tooling, staffing, training, quality controls, SLA improvements, pricing changes, or lead-routing optimization. The target users may include employees, contractors, vendor agents, or community contributors, each with different incentives, constraints, and risk profiles.

Frame this as a strategy decision: clarify the conversion funnel being affected, evaluate strategic options and trade-offs, define the company’s right to win, and identify decision gates for investing, piloting, deferring, or choosing another approach. Consider potential upside from operational leverage and differentiated trust, as well as risks around fairness, gaming, content quality, moderator wellbeing, compliance, and brand safety.

The experience should consider:
- Who the “lead” is, where conversion happens in the funnel, and how moderator behavior could realistically influence it.
- Which moderator segments are in scope, including geography, task type, tenure, employment model, and motivation.
- The strategic options available: build, buy, partner, pilot, or invest in non-reward levers.
- The company’s right to win through data access, platform scale, workflow integration, trust and safety expertise, and measurement capability.
- Trade-offs between conversion lift, moderation quality, cost to serve, speed, compliance, and user trust.
- Risks of reward gaming, perverse incentives, biased moderation outcomes, burnout, or misalignment with safety goals.
- Decision gates, including required evidence, pilot success criteria, budget thresholds, operational readiness, and reasons to stop.

Your goal is to make a clear recommendation on whether to invest, grounded in market logic, user behavior, business impact, strategic fit, measurable risks, and the conditions needed for the decision to be successful.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in forecast accuracy for subscription renewal journey
description:
Problem Statement Description

A marketplace platform provides sellers with a subscription renewal journey, likely covering plan expiration reminders, renewal eligibility, pricing or tier changes, payment attempts, grace periods, and post-renewal status updates. Forecast accuracy for this journey has suddenly dropped, meaning the platform’s predictions of upcoming renewals, churn, revenue, or seller subscription status are materially diverging from actual outcomes.

Your task is to diagnose the issue before proposing any fixes. Treat this as a hard RCA problem where the drop may come from product behavior, seller mix, payment flows, pricing changes, model/data pipeline issues, instrumentation gaps, seasonality, marketplace policy changes, or operational interventions. The key is to frame the anomaly precisely, separate real business movement from measurement or forecasting defects, and identify the most likely root cause through structured evidence.

The experience should consider:
- What “forecast accuracy” means in this context, including prediction window, denominator, error metric, and whether accuracy is measured at seller, subscription, revenue, cohort, or marketplace level
- When the drop started, how sudden it was, and whether it aligns with launches, pricing updates, billing changes, model deployments, data pipeline changes, or seller communications
- Segmentation by seller type, geography, plan tier, tenure, renewal date, payment method, marketplace category, account health, and auto-renew versus manual renewal behavior
- Instrumentation checks across forecast inputs, renewal events, billing status, cancellation events, failed payments, grace-period states, and downstream reporting tables
- Hypotheses that distinguish forecasting-model degradation from actual seller behavior shifts, data freshness issues, label leakage, delayed event processing, or changes in renewal journey completion
- Evidence needed from dashboards, logs, experiment flags, model monitoring, customer-support signals, finance reconciliation, and operational incident reports
- Immediate mitigation options if forecasts are unreliable, including stakeholder communication, temporary reporting caveats, fallback baselines, and risk containment
- Prevention mechanisms such as monitoring, alerting, data contracts, launch checklists, model performance reviews, and ownership of renewal-journey metrics

The goal is to demonstrate a rigorous RCA approach: define the anomaly, validate the measurement, isolate affected cohorts, generate and test hypotheses, identify the root cause with confidence, and only then outline how the team should decide on mitigations and longer-term prevention.

title: Resolve a cross-functional conflict blocking Maps
description:
About Apple
Apple designs and manufactures consumer electronics, software, and services.

Context
Apple Maps is developing a family-oriented experience but faces a cross-functional conflict among various teams. This disagreement is hindering progress and needs resolution to maintain user trust and quality standards.

Prioritization · Planning and sequencing · Stakeholder alignment · Launch criteria

title: Tell me about a time you made a hard trade-off between speed and quality in the context of local delivery experience for marketplace sellers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to describe a real situation where you had to choose between moving quickly and maintaining a high-quality local delivery experience for marketplace sellers. The setting should involve sellers who depend on reliable pickup, handoff, delivery timing, tracking, or issue resolution to fulfill customer orders and protect their business reputation.

Your example should show a meaningful product or operational trade-off, not a routine prioritization decision. The interviewer is looking for evidence that you could operate under pressure, make an informed decision with incomplete information, align stakeholders, and take responsibility for the consequences of the trade-off.

Focus on what made the decision hard: seller impact, buyer trust, delivery partner reliability, launch timing, operational readiness, quality thresholds, or risk of marketplace disruption. The story should make clear what you personally owned, how you evaluated the trade-off, what decision you made, and what happened afterward.

The experience should consider:
- The specific local delivery workflow involved, such as seller onboarding, pickup scheduling, courier assignment, tracking, failed delivery handling, or SLA monitoring
- The seller pain point or business risk created by speed, quality, or reliability constraints
- The options you considered and why none of them were obviously right
- The data, customer signals, operational input, or qualitative evidence you used to make the decision
- How you aligned cross-functional partners such as engineering, operations, support, sales, logistics, or leadership
- The impact on sellers, buyers, marketplace trust, delivery reliability, or business goals
- What you did to monitor, mitigate, or correct issues after the decision
- What you learned and how it changed your approach to future product or operational trade-offs

The goal is to demonstrate sound product judgment in a high-stakes marketplace environment, where speed can unlock business value but poor delivery quality can damage seller trust and marketplace reliability.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling pricing experimentation console for freelancers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale a pricing experimentation console used to test price changes for freelancers who offer appointment-based services. The product goal is to improve appointment attendance, not just bookings or revenue, so the system must support experiments that can measure whether pricing interventions influence customers to actually show up.

The console may be used by product, operations, pricing, data science, and marketplace teams to configure experiments across different freelancer categories, geographies, customer segments, appointment types, and pricing mechanics. Freelancers and customers are indirectly affected through price displays, booking flows, reminders, cancellation policies, and payments, so reliability and trust are critical.

As a Technical PM, your task is to evaluate the technical trade-offs involved in scaling this experimentation platform. Focus on what requirements, architecture choices, data flows, privacy controls, rollout mechanisms, and observability are needed to support safe, trustworthy, and decision-useful pricing experiments at scale.

The experience should consider:
- How experiment configuration, targeting, eligibility, and assignment would work across freelancers, customers, appointment types, regions, and time windows
- APIs and data dependencies needed between pricing, booking, payments, attendance tracking, notifications, analytics, and freelancer-facing systems
- Reliability requirements for price calculation and display, especially when experiments affect live customer booking decisions
- Privacy, security, and fairness considerations when using customer, freelancer, location, behavioral, or historical attendance data
- How to prevent conflicting experiments, inconsistent pricing, customer confusion, or freelancer trust issues
- Observability needs, including exposure logging, price shown, booking completion, appointment attendance, cancellations, no-shows, refunds, and downstream complaints
- Rollout strategy, including feature flags, holdouts, staged launches, fallback behavior, incident response, and rollback criteria
- Product trade-offs between experimentation velocity, statistical rigor, operational simplicity, marketplace fairness, and user trust

Your goal is to frame a technically sound evaluation of how this pricing experimentation console should scale while protecting the freelancer marketplace experience and producing reliable evidence about appointment attendance outcomes.

title: Create a launch plan for fraud alert experience aimed at delivery partners
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are responsible for launching a fraud alert experience for delivery partners in a large-scale delivery marketplace. The experience is intended to notify partners when suspicious activity, policy violations, account risks, or potentially fraudulent delivery patterns require their attention, and to drive them toward the appropriate next action.

The launch must optimize for conversion, meaning delivery partners not only see and understand the alert, but complete the intended action flow—such as acknowledging the alert, verifying information, submitting evidence, correcting behavior, or resolving an account-risk issue. The plan should account for the fact that delivery partners are often on the move, time-constrained, earnings-sensitive, and may distrust unclear fraud messaging.

This is an execution-focused question. Your task is to define how you would take the experience from readiness to rollout, including sequencing, operational ownership, dependencies, success criteria, launch risks, communication, and post-launch iteration. You should not redesign the fraud system itself, but you should consider how the alert experience, rollout process, and partner communication affect conversion.

The experience should consider:
- Target delivery partner segments, including new partners, high-volume partners, previously flagged partners, and partners in different markets or languages
- Launch sequencing, such as internal testing, limited-market pilots, staged rollout, and full-scale release
- Key owners and dependencies across product, engineering, risk, legal, operations, support, communications, and analytics
- Conversion funnel definition from alert exposure to successful completion of the required action
- Go/no-go criteria, guardrail metrics, escalation paths, and rollback triggers
- Partner communication strategy, including timing, tone, channels, and clarity of required action
- Support and operations readiness for partner confusion, disputes, false positives, or appeals
- Post-launch monitoring, experimentation, iteration cadence, and learnings needed to improve conversion without harming trust

The goal is to present a practical launch plan that can safely introduce a sensitive fraud-related experience, improve completion of required partner actions, protect marketplace integrity, and minimize unnecessary disruption to legitimate delivery partners.

title: Design a B2B onboarding console for privacy-conscious users that improves renewal confidence
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are designing a B2B onboarding console for organizations that are highly sensitive to privacy, data access, compliance, and vendor risk. The console is used after a customer signs a contract but before they are fully live, helping admins, security reviewers, legal/compliance stakeholders, and business sponsors understand what needs to be configured, approved, integrated, and verified.

The key product challenge is that onboarding friction can reduce confidence long before renewal discussions begin. Privacy-conscious customers may delay rollout if they do not understand what data is collected, who can access it, how integrations behave, or whether internal policy requirements have been met. At the same time, vendor-side customer success and implementation teams need visibility into progress without creating more manual coordination or exposing unnecessary customer information.

Design the product experience for this onboarding console with a focus on building trust, reducing uncertainty, and helping customers feel confident that the product is safe, well-governed, and delivering value by the time renewal decisions are considered. Assume this is a B2B SaaS environment with multiple customer stakeholders, enterprise procurement/security expectations, and a need to support repeatable onboarding across many accounts.

The experience should consider:
- The primary users and stakeholders involved in onboarding, including admins, privacy/security reviewers, business owners, and vendor-side teams.
- The end-to-end onboarding workflow from kickoff through configuration, integration, approvals, launch readiness, and early adoption.
- Privacy-specific friction points such as data sharing clarity, permissioning, auditability, consent, retention, compliance evidence, and access controls.
- How the console helps customers track progress, understand blockers, and know what actions are required from whom.
- How trust and renewal confidence can be supported without overwhelming users with legal, technical, or compliance complexity.
- How the experience adapts for different customer sizes, industries, maturity levels, and internal approval processes.
- What signals or moments would indicate that onboarding is successful and that the customer is likely to feel confident continuing the relationship.

Your goal is to define a clear product experience that makes onboarding feel transparent, controlled, and outcome-oriented for privacy-conscious B2B customers, while also supporting the business objective of stronger renewal confidence.

title: Create a launch plan for AI sales assistant aimed at new users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are planning the launch of an AI sales assistant for new users who are expected to onboard and achieve value without hands-on help from a sales or customer success team. The assistant may help users understand prospects, draft outreach, prioritize leads, summarize conversations, or recommend next actions, but the launch focus is not on defining the full product vision—it is on getting new users to self-serve activation successfully.

The challenge is to create an execution plan that turns a potentially complex AI workflow into a reliable, trustworthy first-use experience. New users may arrive with limited context, incomplete data, unclear expectations of AI quality, and varying levels of sales process maturity. The launch plan should account for onboarding, education, setup, adoption, support, measurement, risk management, and cross-functional coordination.

Assume this is a real product launch where product, engineering, design, marketing, sales, support, legal, data science, and operations may all have roles. The plan should clarify what needs to happen before launch, during rollout, and after launch to determine whether new users are succeeding through self-serve usage.

The experience should consider:
- The target new-user workflow from signup through first meaningful AI-assisted sales outcome
- Launch sequencing, including beta, limited rollout, general availability, and expansion criteria
- Owners, dependencies, and coordination across product, engineering, design, data, GTM, support, and legal
- Go/no-go criteria such as activation quality, AI reliability, onboarding completion, support burden, and trust signals
- Self-serve enablement including onboarding, templates, examples, in-product guidance, help content, and escalation paths
- Instrumentation needed to track activation, usage, drop-offs, AI output quality, user confidence, and retention
- Risks around inaccurate AI recommendations, poor data setup, privacy, compliance, user disappointment, and operational overload
- Rollback, mitigation, and communication plans if launch quality or user outcomes fall below expectations

The goal is to produce a clear, practical launch plan that maximizes new-user self-serve success while managing execution risk, ensuring accountable ownership, and creating feedback loops to improve the AI sales assistant after launch.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for marketplace quality score among delivery partners
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the annual opportunity of introducing or improving a marketplace quality score for delivery partners in a large-scale delivery marketplace. The quality score is intended to help the platform identify, guide, and reward delivery partners based on behaviors that affect customer trust, merchant reliability, and operational efficiency.

Frame the estimate as a business opportunity: what value could be created in one year if the score meaningfully improves delivery partner performance or marketplace matching decisions. You should connect the opportunity to time to value, including how quickly the platform might begin seeing measurable impact after rollout and what adoption or operational dependencies could slow it down.

Your estimate should be grounded in a clear marketplace workflow: delivery partners accept orders, pick up items, deliver to customers, and generate quality signals such as timeliness, cancellations, complaints, order handling, communication, and repeat reliability. Focus on the annualized impact of using these signals to improve outcomes, not on designing the scoring algorithm itself.

The experience should consider:
- Scope of the marketplace, including active delivery partners, order volume, markets covered, and relevant delivery categories.
- Unit of value, such as incremental completed orders, reduced refunds/support costs, improved retention, higher customer repeat rate, or better partner productivity.
- Population segmentation, including new vs. experienced partners, high-volume vs. occasional partners, and low-quality vs. high-quality cohorts.
- Adoption and frequency assumptions, such as how often partners receive score feedback and how often dispatch or incentives use the score.
- Time-to-value assumptions, including onboarding time, behavior-change lag, marketplace policy rollout, and measurement windows.
- Key assumptions and sensitivities, especially around baseline defect rates, achievable improvement, partner responsiveness, and operational cost.
- Sanity checks to ensure the annual opportunity is plausible relative to marketplace scale and current economics.

The goal is to produce a structured, transparent estimate that shows how you size the opportunity, what assumptions drive the result, and how you would judge whether the marketplace quality score creates value quickly enough to justify investment.

title: Plan reliability, privacy, and monitoring for payments checkout
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the Technical PM for a payments checkout experience used by local merchants to accept customer payments across web, mobile, and in-store assisted flows. The checkout must be fast and dependable during peak sales periods, while also protecting sensitive payment and customer data. Merchants depend on successful transactions for revenue, and even brief outages, confusing failures, or privacy incidents can damage trust.

In this interview, you are asked to plan the reliability, privacy, and monitoring approach for the checkout system. Assume the product integrates with payment processors, fraud/risk systems, merchant dashboards, customer notifications, and internal support tools. Your scope includes defining what the product and platform should require from APIs, data handling, observability, alerting, incident response, and rollout readiness.

The experience should consider:
- Key checkout flows and failure points, including payment authorization, confirmation, retries, timeouts, and post-payment reconciliation
- Reliability expectations such as uptime, latency, error rates, graceful degradation, idempotency, and recovery from third-party provider issues
- Privacy and security requirements for payment data, customer identity, merchant information, logs, analytics, and internal access
- Monitoring and instrumentation needed to detect checkout failures, conversion drops, duplicate charges, delayed confirmations, and processor-specific anomalies
- Operational workflows for alerts, dashboards, incident ownership, escalation, merchant communication, and support investigation
- Rollout considerations such as phased launches, feature flags, backward compatibility, regional/payment-method differences, and rollback criteria
- Product trade-offs between checkout speed, fraud prevention, data minimization, compliance needs, and merchant/customer transparency

Your goal is to frame a practical Technical PM plan that helps local merchants achieve high checkout success while maintaining customer trust, regulatory readiness, and strong operational visibility.

title: Handle conflicting stakeholder asks for voice assistant flow
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the PM responsible for a voice assistant workflow used by healthcare coordinators to complete tasks hands-free while moving between patient rooms, reviewing schedules, updating care status, and coordinating follow-ups. The team is preparing to ship an improved voice flow, but key stakeholders are pushing for conflicting changes: clinical operations wants fewer confirmation steps to reduce time per task, compliance wants stricter consent and audit capture, design wants a more natural conversational flow, engineering wants to limit scope due to reliability risks, and customer success is escalating requests from large healthcare customers.

This is an execution-focused scenario. Your role is to bring structure to the conflict, align stakeholders on what must ship, define the operating plan, and manage launch risk without assuming unlimited time, engineering capacity, or tolerance for clinical errors. The product must support high-trust, accessible, hands-free task completion in a healthcare environment where misrecognition, interruptions, background noise, privacy concerns, and workflow urgency all matter.

The experience should consider:
- The core healthcare coordinator workflows affected by the voice assistant flow and where hands-free completion is most valuable
- Stakeholder asks, underlying motivations, non-negotiables, and areas where trade-offs are possible
- Owners, decision rights, dependencies, and how disagreements will be resolved before launch
- Sequencing of requirements, including what belongs in the initial release versus later iterations
- Go/no-go criteria for quality, safety, compliance, usability, and operational readiness
- Rollback or fallback plans if the voice flow causes errors, user confusion, or workflow disruption
- Communication plans for internal teams, pilot customers, support, and healthcare coordinator users
- Launch risks related to reliability, privacy, accessibility, training, and adoption in clinical settings

Your goal is to explain how you would execute through the stakeholder conflict and ship a responsible voice assistant flow that improves hands-free completion for healthcare coordinators while managing operational, technical, compliance, and user-experience risks.

title: Create a launch plan for remote training platform aimed at fleet coordinators
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are launching a remote training platform for fleet coordinators who manage driver schedules, vehicle readiness, route changes, compliance tasks, incident follow-up, and day-to-day operational exceptions. These users are often time-constrained, distributed across depots or regions, and measured on operational continuity rather than training completion alone.

The platform is intended to help coordinators become productive quickly on new processes, tools, safety/compliance requirements, and operational playbooks without requiring in-person classroom sessions. The launch plan should focus on reducing time to value: how quickly coordinators can access the right training, complete critical modules, apply the learning in real workflows, and show measurable operational improvement.

Assume the product is ready for an initial launch, but adoption, manager buy-in, content readiness, support capacity, and operational disruption are key risks. Your task is to define how you would take this product to market, sequence rollout activities, align stakeholders, measure readiness, and decide whether to expand, pause, or roll back.

The experience should consider:

- Target launch segments, such as region, fleet size, coordinator seniority, operational complexity, or training urgency
- Onboarding workflow from invite to first useful training outcome, including account setup, content assignment, reminders, and manager visibility
- Operating plan across product, training/content, customer success, fleet operations, support, analytics, and legal/compliance stakeholders
- Dependencies such as training content availability, LMS or HR system integrations, mobile/desktop access, permissions, localization, and reporting
- Go/no-go criteria for pilot, phased rollout, and broader launch based on readiness, adoption, completion, satisfaction, and operational impact
- Launch risks, including low engagement, scheduling conflicts, poor content relevance, connectivity issues, compliance gaps, and frontline support overload
- Communication and enablement plan for coordinators, their managers, depot leaders, and internal teams
- Rollback or mitigation approach if the launch causes confusion, operational delays, inaccurate reporting, or poor learning outcomes

Your goal is to present a practical launch plan that gets fleet coordinators to meaningful value quickly while protecting day-to-day fleet operations. Focus on sequencing, ownership, measurable checkpoints, risk management, and the decisions you would make before, during, and after launch.

title: Redesign the end-to-end small business cash-flow assistant journey to increase actionable cash-flow task completion rate
description:
Problem Statement Description

Intuit serves many first-time business owners who are learning how to manage invoices, expenses, payroll, taxes, and cash reserves while running day-to-day operations. A small business cash-flow assistant can help them understand what is coming in, what is going out, and what actions they should take next, but the current end-to-end journey is not driving enough completion of actionable cash-flow tasks.

Your task is to redesign the user experience for this assistant with the goal of increasing the rate at which small business owners complete meaningful cash-flow actions, such as following up on overdue invoices, scheduling bill payments, setting aside money for taxes, reviewing upcoming shortfalls, or adjusting spending plans. Focus on the full workflow from onboarding and data connection through insight discovery, recommendation, decision-making, and task completion.

Assume the target users are financially anxious, time-constrained, and may not have strong accounting knowledge. The experience must build trust, explain recommendations clearly, and avoid making users feel judged or overwhelmed. It should also respect the sensitivity of financial data and the consequences of inaccurate or poorly timed guidance.

The experience should consider:
- How first-time business owners discover, understand, and start using the cash-flow assistant
- What data the assistant needs, how users connect or verify it, and how to handle missing or low-quality data
- How cash-flow insights are prioritized so users know what requires attention now versus later
- How recommendations become clear, actionable tasks rather than passive financial observations
- How the product explains assumptions, confidence, and trade-offs behind cash-flow guidance
- How to support trust, privacy, accessibility, and compliance-sensitive financial interactions
- How to reduce friction across reminders, approvals, task execution, and follow-up confirmation
- How to measure whether users are becoming more confident and taking healthier financial actions

Your goal is to define a redesigned product journey that helps first-time business owners move from uncertainty to informed action, while increasing actionable cash-flow task completion in a way that is trustworthy, understandable, and appropriate for Intuit’s small business finance ecosystem.

title: Prioritize the next strategic bet in learning platform under constrained investment
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the next strategic bet for a learning platform that serves privacy-conscious users and wants to improve course or learning-path completion. The company has limited investment capacity, so it cannot pursue every promising opportunity at once. Your task is to frame how the product team should choose among competing strategic options without assuming unlimited engineering, content, data science, or go-to-market resources.

The platform likely includes learners discovering courses, enrolling, progressing through lessons, receiving reminders or recommendations, and completing assessments or certificates. Privacy-conscious users may be especially sensitive to data collection, personalization, tracking, AI-driven recommendations, third-party integrations, or social/community features. This creates tension between improving engagement and completion while preserving trust, transparency, and user control.

This is a strategy interview question. Focus on how you would structure the decision, compare opportunities, reason through trade-offs, and define what evidence would justify prioritizing one strategic bet over another. Do not jump directly to a feature idea; clarify the market, user segment, business objective, constraints, and decision criteria first.

The experience should consider:
- The target learner segment, including what “privacy-conscious” means in behavior, expectations, and willingness to share data
- The completion problem: where learners drop off, why completion matters, and how completion connects to business value
- Strategic options available to a learning platform, such as content quality, motivation, personalization, credentials, community, enterprise use cases, or privacy-first trust features
- Investment constraints across engineering effort, content operations, data infrastructure, compliance, marketing, and support
- Trade-offs between growth, learner outcomes, trust, monetization, accessibility, and operational complexity
- The company’s right to win based on existing assets, brand trust, distribution, learning data, partnerships, or platform capabilities
- Risks and decision gates, including privacy risk, low adoption, weak completion impact, regulatory concerns, or limited differentiation
- How success would be validated before scaling the chosen bet

Your goal is to present a clear strategic recommendation process for selecting the next investment area, including how you would evaluate options, what assumptions you would test, and what evidence would convince you to commit scarce resources.

title: Create a launch plan for workflow automation builder aimed at healthcare coordinators
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager responsible for launching a workflow automation builder for healthcare coordinators. The product is intended to help coordinators create and manage automated workflows that improve appointment attendance, such as reminders, follow-ups, rescheduling questions, eligibility checks, transportation nudges, or care-team escalations.

Healthcare coordinators operate in a high-friction environment: patients miss appointments for many reasons, providers have limited capacity, communication channels vary by patient, and workflows often depend on EHR data, scheduling systems, consent rules, and care-team handoffs. Your launch plan should focus on how to introduce this builder safely and effectively into coordinator workflows while improving attendance without increasing operational burden.

This is an execution-focused question. You are not being asked to design the full product from scratch or choose a long-term company strategy. Instead, define how you would take the product to launch, align teams, sequence work, manage dependencies, measure readiness, reduce risk, and ensure the launch drives measurable improvement in appointment attendance.

The experience should consider:
- Target users and launch scope, including which coordinator teams, appointment types, patient segments, or care settings are included first
- Key workflows the builder must support at launch, such as reminder automation, missed-appointment follow-up, rescheduling, escalation, and patient communication preferences
- Cross-functional owners and dependencies across product, engineering, design, clinical operations, legal/compliance, data, support, implementation, and customer success
- Sequencing of the launch plan, including pilot design, configuration, training, data integrations, QA, rollout phases, and operational readiness
- Go/no-go criteria tied to workflow reliability, coordinator adoption, patient communication success, compliance readiness, and appointment attendance impact
- Risk management for healthcare-specific concerns such as PHI handling, consent, message fatigue, incorrect outreach, integration failures, accessibility, and care-team accountability
- Measurement and reporting plan, including leading indicators, outcome metrics, guardrails, cohort tracking, and post-launch review cadence
- Rollback, mitigation, and communication plans if workflows create errors, patient confusion, operational overload, or no measurable attendance improvement

Your goal is to present a clear, practical launch plan that shows how you would coordinate execution from pilot through broader rollout, while protecting patient trust, supporting healthcare coordinators, and improving appointment attendance in a measurable and responsible way.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for admin audit log among warehouse managers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the annual opportunity for an admin audit log feature used by warehouse managers. These managers oversee day-to-day warehouse operations, supervise staff actions, resolve exceptions, manage inventory or shipment workflows, and often need to understand who changed what, when, and why inside warehouse management or operations software.

The estimate should quantify the potential annual value or usage opportunity for audit logs in this segment, while explicitly connecting the estimate to workflow completion. For example, the audit log may help managers resolve blocked workflows, investigate errors, approve corrections, reduce rework, maintain compliance, or restore accountability when operational tasks fail or are delayed.

This is a guesstimate exercise, so the focus is not on knowing the exact market size. The candidate should define a reasonable scope, make transparent assumptions, size the relevant user population and usage frequency, and translate audit-log usage into a meaningful annual opportunity tied to completed warehouse workflows.

The experience should consider:
- The target population, such as number of warehouses, warehouse managers per site, or software-enabled warehouses in scope
- The unit of opportunity, such as annual users, audit-log sessions, resolved workflow exceptions, time saved, revenue potential, or cost avoidance
- How often warehouse managers encounter workflow-blocking issues that require traceability
- Adoption assumptions for admin audit logs within warehouse management systems or operational SaaS tools
- The relationship between audit-log access and workflow completion, including reduced investigation time, fewer escalations, or faster approvals
- Segmentation by warehouse size, operational complexity, region, industry, or digitization level
- Key assumptions, sensitivity drivers, and sanity checks to test whether the estimate is plausible
- Constraints such as limited software adoption, role-based access, compliance requirements, and data quality

The goal is to produce a structured, defensible annual estimate and clearly explain how the opportunity is created through improved completion of warehouse management workflows, rather than treating the audit log as an isolated administrative feature.

title: Decide what to cut from a delayed fraud detection workflow launch
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the PM responsible for launching a delayed fraud detection workflow designed to reduce risk for family accounts, such as shared payment methods, child or teen profiles, household subscriptions, marketplace purchases, or caregiver-managed access. The workflow is intended to detect suspicious activity, route cases for review or user verification, and help families recover safely without creating unnecessary friction for legitimate users.

The launch has slipped, and leadership is asking you to decide what to cut, defer, or simplify so the team can still ship a safe and useful version. Engineering, operations, policy, legal, support, data science, and design teams are involved, and some components may be incomplete, such as automated risk scoring, manual review tooling, user notifications, appeals, localization, reporting dashboards, or edge-case handling.

This is an execution decision under ambiguity. You need to show how you would protect users and the business while making pragmatic scope trade-offs, sequencing the remaining work, aligning stakeholders, and defining clear criteria for launch readiness.

The experience should consider:
- The core user and operational workflows that must work on day one for family fraud detection, review, notification, and resolution.
- Which components are safety-critical, compliance-critical, trust-critical, or operationally nice-to-have.
- Owners, dependencies, staffing constraints, and sequencing across product, engineering, risk, operations, support, policy, and legal.
- Go/no-go criteria for launch, including acceptable false positives, false negatives, review backlog, latency, coverage, and escalation readiness.
- Rollout approach, such as internal testing, limited cohorts, geography or segment phasing, and controlled exposure.
- Mitigation plans for launch risks, including user harm, account lockouts, delayed reviews, support overload, model errors, and abuse adaptation.
- Rollback, monitoring, communications, and incident response plans if the workflow performs poorly after release.

Your goal is to describe how you would make and communicate the cut decisions, preserve the minimum viable risk-reduction outcome for families, and create an operating plan that allows the launch to proceed responsibly without hiding material safety or trust risks.

title: Plan reliability, privacy, and monitoring for local delivery experience
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the Technical PM for a local delivery experience used by marketplace sellers to offer same-day or scheduled delivery to nearby buyers. Sellers depend on this experience to create delivery promises, hand off orders to couriers or logistics partners, track status, resolve exceptions, and communicate accurate updates to buyers. The system operates across multiple actors—seller tools, buyer-facing checkout and tracking, courier apps, partner APIs, payment/refund systems, and support workflows.

The interview asks you to plan the reliability, privacy, and monitoring approach for this experience. Focus on how the product and technical system should behave when delivery promises are made, orders are assigned, locations are shared, status events are delayed or missing, partners degrade, and buyers or sellers need trustworthy visibility. You should consider both the seller-facing workflow and the underlying platform responsibilities needed to operate at scale.

This is a technical product management problem, so your response should connect product requirements with APIs, data flows, service boundaries, operational controls, privacy constraints, observability, rollout strategy, and trade-offs. Do not assume a greenfield system only; consider that the local delivery experience may depend on third-party logistics providers, internal marketplace services, and real-time event streams with varying reliability.

The experience should consider:
- Critical user journeys for marketplace sellers, buyers, couriers, support agents, and delivery partners.
- Reliability expectations for checkout delivery promises, order assignment, live tracking, status updates, cancellations, retries, and exception handling.
- Privacy requirements for location data, buyer/seller contact details, delivery addresses, courier identity, retention, access control, and consent.
- APIs, event schemas, data contracts, idempotency, fallback behavior, and partner integration failure modes.
- Monitoring for latency, availability, event freshness, delivery state accuracy, SLA breaches, data quality, and user-visible incidents.
- Alerting, incident response, escalation paths, dashboards, audit logs, and post-incident prevention mechanisms.
- Rollout, experimentation, backward compatibility, operational readiness, and safe degradation when dependencies fail.
- Product trade-offs between real-time precision, cost, complexity, seller trust, buyer transparency, and privacy risk.

Your goal is to define a clear technical product plan that enables a dependable, privacy-conscious local delivery experience for marketplace sellers while giving the business enough observability and control to detect issues early, protect sensitive data, and maintain customer trust during normal operations and failure scenarios.

title: Define success metrics for developer platform serving mobile-first users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a developer platform whose customers are teams building mobile-first products, such as consumer apps, marketplace apps, fintech apps, or SaaS companion apps. These teams use the platform’s SDKs, APIs, documentation, dashboards, sandbox tools, and support channels to integrate platform capabilities into iOS, Android, or mobile web experiences.

The interview asks you to define what “success” means for this platform from a metrics perspective. The core outcome is integration success: whether developers can discover the platform, onboard, build, test, launch, and maintain reliable integrations that work well for mobile-first end users.

Your answer should focus on building a useful measurement framework rather than naming isolated vanity metrics. Consider the full developer journey, the business value of successful integrations, and the quality of the downstream mobile experience.

The experience should consider:
- Clear metric definitions, including numerators, denominators, and time windows.
- Developer funnel stages from sign-up to first API call, successful SDK implementation, test completion, production launch, and sustained usage.
- Mobile-specific integration quality, including SDK stability, latency, crash impact, app size, device coverage, network variability, and OS/version compatibility.
- Cohorts such as new vs. existing developers, company size, platform used, geography, integration type, and mobile operating system.
- Instrumentation needed across docs, developer console, SDKs, APIs, sandbox, support, and production traffic.
- Guardrail metrics for reliability, security, privacy, abuse, support burden, and end-user experience.
- Decision usefulness: how the metrics would help product, engineering, developer relations, and business teams prioritize improvements.

The goal is to define a balanced success-measurement system that shows whether the developer platform is helping mobile-first teams integrate quickly, launch confidently, and maintain high-quality production experiences over time.

title: Estimate the operational cost of scaling subscription billing to multiple regions
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are asked to estimate the operational cost of expanding a subscription billing system from a single-region setup to multiple regions for a large-scale digital product serving students. The billing experience supports recurring payments, discounts or student pricing, renewals, failed-payment recovery, refunds, tax handling, and customer support workflows across different geographies.

The estimate should focus on incremental operational cost, not total company cost. Consider what new recurring effort, tooling, vendors, compliance processes, support coverage, payment operations, and monitoring may be required when billing students in multiple regions with different payment methods, currencies, regulations, taxes, and failure patterns.

This is a guesstimate exercise, so the expectation is not a precise financial model. The important part is defining the scope clearly, choosing reasonable units, making transparent assumptions, and showing how the cost estimate would change under different scale or complexity scenarios.

The experience should consider:
- The scope of “multiple regions,” such as number of countries or regional clusters, currencies, languages, and payment ecosystems included.
- The relevant unit of estimation, such as cost per region, cost per active subscriber, cost per transaction, cost per billing incident, or cost per support contact.
- The student subscriber base, including expected adoption, payment frequency, renewal cycles, churn, failed payments, and seasonal patterns tied to academic calendars.
- Key operational cost categories, including payment processing operations, fraud and chargeback handling, tax and compliance operations, customer support, localization, reconciliation, and billing reliability monitoring.
- Dependencies on third-party vendors such as payment gateways, tax engines, identity or student-verification providers, and customer support platforms.
- Assumptions around revenue recovery, including how failed-payment retries, dunning, grace periods, and regional payment preferences affect operational workload.
- Sensitivity to major drivers such as subscriber volume, number of regions, support contact rate, payment failure rate, refund rate, and compliance complexity.
- Sanity checks against comparable SaaS, consumer subscription, or education-technology billing operations to ensure the estimate is directionally credible.

Your goal is to produce a structured, defensible estimate of the annual or monthly operational cost required to run multi-region subscription billing for students, while clearly explaining assumptions, calculation logic, major cost drivers, and where the estimate is most uncertain.

title: Design a voice note capture for procurement teams that improves payment reliability
description:
Problem Statement Description

Procurement teams often work across warehouses, vendor calls, site visits, email threads, purchase orders, invoices, and approval systems. Critical payment details can be captured informally in conversations, especially when buyers or operations teams are away from their desks. Design a voice note capture experience that helps procurement users record, organize, and convert those verbal details into reliable payment-related workflows.

The product should focus on reducing friction and errors that lead to late, missed, duplicate, or disputed payments. Consider how procurement managers, buyers, approvers, accounts payable partners, and vendors might interact with the captured information before a payment is approved or released.

Your design should account for real-world procurement environments: noisy settings, multilingual teams, urgent vendor escalations, incomplete context, policy requirements, and the need to connect spoken notes back to purchase orders, goods receipts, invoices, approvals, and payment status.

The experience should consider:
- Who the primary users are and when they would capture voice notes in the procurement workflow
- What payment reliability means in this context and which user pain points matter most
- How voice notes should be structured, reviewed, corrected, and linked to procurement records
- How the product handles ambiguity, missing information, accents, background noise, and multilingual input
- How teams build trust in captured data before it affects payment decisions
- What permissions, auditability, privacy, and compliance expectations are important
- How the experience fits into existing procurement, ERP, or accounts payable tools
- What success indicators would show that payment reliability has improved

The goal is to define a clear product experience that makes it easier for procurement teams to capture important payment-related context at the moment it occurs, while ensuring that the information becomes accurate, actionable, and trustworthy enough to support downstream payment operations.

title: Plan the MVP rollout for Insurance in a constrained market
description:
About Tesla
Tesla designs and manufactures electric vehicles and energy products.

Context
Tesla is launching an MVP of its Insurance product for safety-conscious families. The rollout must navigate regulatory and operational constraints while ensuring customer trust and a consistent experience with Tesla's ecosystem.

Key details
- Users: safety-conscious families
- Product: Insurance MVP
- Situation: launching in a constrained market
- Goal: execute a phased rollout plan

How you'll be evaluated
Prioritization · Planning and sequencing · Stakeholder alignment · Launch criteria

title: Create a launch plan for document collaboration flow aimed at finance teams
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are launching a new document collaboration flow for finance teams who prepare, review, approve, and hand off high-stakes documents such as budgets, forecasts, board materials, close packages, audit support, and variance analyses. These workflows often involve analysts, finance managers, controllers, FP&A leaders, legal/compliance partners, and executives, with strict deadlines and a low tolerance for version confusion, missing context, or unauthorized changes.

The launch needs to improve handoff quality: when ownership moves from one person or team to another, the recipient should understand what changed, what decisions were made, what remains open, what approvals are required, and whether the document is ready for the next step. The plan should account for complex collaboration patterns, sensitive financial data, auditability expectations, and cross-functional dependencies.

You are not being asked to design the full product solution. Focus on how you would take the collaboration flow from readiness to launch and adoption, including sequencing, owners, risks, rollout controls, measurement, and communication.

The experience should consider:
- Which finance workflows and user roles are in scope for launch, and which should be excluded or deferred.
