title: Create a launch plan for personalized pricing guardrail aimed at team leads
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are asked to create an execution-focused launch plan for a personalized pricing guardrail used by team leads. The guardrail is intended to help team leads review, enforce, or intervene in pricing decisions that may vary by customer, account, geography, usage, or segment, while ensuring that the content presented to users remains high quality, accurate, consistent, and trustworthy.

Assume team leads are operational owners who oversee pricing recommendations, approvals, exceptions, or customer-facing pricing content produced by internal tools, sales workflows, marketplace systems, or AI-assisted experiences. Their pain points may include inconsistent pricing explanations, low-quality generated content, unclear exception handling, slow review cycles, insufficient auditability, and risk of unfair or confusing customer experiences.

Your task is not to design the pricing algorithm itself, but to plan how this guardrail should be launched safely and effectively. The launch plan should cover how the product, operations, policy, data, engineering, and go-to-market teams coordinate to roll out the capability, measure quality, handle risks, and decide when to expand, pause, or roll back.

The experience should consider:
- The intended workflow for team leads before, during, and after pricing content review or approval
- Clear owners across product, engineering, data science, policy/legal, operations, support, and enablement
- Dependencies such as pricing rules, content-quality evaluation, audit logs, permissions, dashboards, and training materials
- Sequencing from internal testing to pilot, limited rollout, broader launch, and post-launch monitoring
- Go/no-go criteria tied to content quality, accuracy, consistency, fairness, latency, operational load, and customer trust
- Rollback and escalation paths for incorrect pricing, poor-quality explanations, policy violations, or team-lead override failures
- Communication plans for team leads, adjacent teams, leadership, and impacted customer-facing roles

Your goal is to present a practical launch plan that shows how you would operationalize the personalized pricing guardrail with disciplined execution, measurable quality controls, clear accountability, and thoughtful risk management while keeping the team-lead workflow effective and scalable.

title: Improve the first-week AI writing assistant experience for first-time buyers
description:
Problem Statement Description

A user has just paid for an AI writing assistant for the first time and is entering their first week with the product. They may be trying to write emails, blog drafts, marketing copy, resumes, reports, or other high-stakes content, but they are still learning what the assistant can do, how to ask for better outputs, and how much they can trust the results.

Design an improved first-week experience that helps these first-time buyers quickly reach useful, high-quality writing outcomes. The focus is not just activation or feature discovery, but reducing the friction between “I bought this tool” and “I produced something I’m confident using.” Consider the emotional state of new buyers: curiosity, urgency, skepticism, fear of wasting money, and concern about originality, tone, accuracy, and privacy.

Your response should define the target user segment, their key first-week jobs-to-be-done, the moments where quality breaks down, and the product experience that should support better outcomes. You may assume the product already has core AI writing capabilities, but the onboarding, guidance, editing flow, trust-building, and feedback loops can be improved.

The experience should consider:
- The first-time buyer’s workflow from purchase through first meaningful writing output
- Common reasons generated content may feel low quality, generic, inaccurate, off-brand, or unusable
- How users express intent, context, tone, audience, constraints, and source material to the assistant
- How the product helps users evaluate, refine, and confidently use AI-generated writing
- Differences across use cases such as professional writing, personal writing, academic-style drafting, or marketing content
- Responsible AI expectations, including privacy, plagiarism concerns, factual accuracy, and appropriate disclosure
- Accessibility and ease of use for users who may not be question-writing experts
- Signals that indicate whether the first-week experience is successfully creating quality output

The goal is to propose a thoughtful product design direction that improves early buyer confidence, reduces time-to-value, and increases the likelihood that users create writing they are satisfied enough to keep, edit, export, or publish.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in self-serve success for partner integration marketplace
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager for a partner integration marketplace used by finance teams to connect tools such as accounting systems, billing platforms, ERP software, spend management, payroll, tax, or reporting products. The marketplace is designed to let finance users discover an integration, authorize the required systems, configure mappings or permissions, test the connection, and complete setup without help from sales, support, or implementation teams.

A sudden drop has been observed in self-serve success. In this context, self-serve success means that a finance team can complete an intended integration workflow without contacting support, abandoning the flow, or requiring manual intervention. Your task is to diagnose what may be causing the drop before recommending any fixes.

This is an RCA exercise. Focus on how you would frame the incident, validate whether the drop is real, isolate where and for whom it is happening, generate hypotheses, gather evidence, and decide what needs immediate mitigation versus deeper follow-up.

The experience should consider:
- How “self-serve success” is defined, including the numerator, denominator, time window, and completion criteria.
- Whether the anomaly is real or caused by tracking, logging, attribution, data freshness, bot filtering, or dashboard changes.
- Segmentation by integration partner, finance system type, customer size, geography, browser/device, account age, user role, and setup step.
- Funnel analysis across discovery, eligibility checks, authorization, permission consent, field mapping, data sync, validation, and final activation.
- Potential causes such as partner API outages, authentication changes, permission scope issues, configuration complexity, UX regressions, pricing or eligibility changes, or support deflection changes.
- Evidence sources including event logs, error codes, partner status pages, release timelines, customer tickets, session replays, conversion cohorts, and operational metrics.
- How to prioritize investigation based on user impact, revenue risk, compliance sensitivity, partner importance, and reversibility.
- What mitigation, communication, monitoring, and prevention mechanisms should be considered once the root cause is understood.

Your goal is to walk through a structured diagnosis that distinguishes correlation from causation, narrows the problem to the most likely affected surfaces and users, and produces a clear path to evidence-backed next steps without jumping prematurely to a solution.

title: Estimate the operational cost of scaling profile and identity flow to multiple regions
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the cost implications of expanding a profile and identity verification flow from a single-region setup to multiple geographic regions. The flow supports community managers who need to onboard, verify, and activate members or contributors while maintaining trust, compliance, and a smooth user experience.

Your task is to estimate the operational cost of this regional scaling effort. Focus on the recurring and incremental costs required to support verified activation across regions, including infrastructure, identity checks, moderation/review operations, support, localization, compliance, monitoring, and reliability needs.

This is a guesstimate, so the emphasis is on structuring the problem clearly, choosing reasonable assumptions, defining the unit of cost, and showing how different adoption, verification, and operating-model assumptions affect the estimate.

The experience should consider:
- Scope: which parts of the profile and identity flow are included, such as account creation, profile completion, document or biometric verification, fraud checks, manual review, and activation.
- Unit of estimation: whether cost is calculated per region, per month, per verified activation, per active community manager, or as an annual operating cost.
- Population and demand: number of regions, expected communities, users entering the identity flow, completion rates, and verification volumes.
- Adoption and frequency: how often users need verification, re-verification, profile updates, support intervention, or manual review.
- Cost drivers: cloud infrastructure, third-party identity verification vendors, human review teams, customer support, fraud/risk operations, localization, legal/compliance, and regional monitoring.
- Assumptions and sensitivity: which variables most affect the estimate, such as verification pass rate, manual review percentage, region-specific compliance burden, and peak traffic.
- Sanity checks: comparing bottom-up cost per user or verification against top-down regional operating budgets and expected business value from verified activation.

The goal is to produce a clear, defensible estimate that helps a product and operations team understand the likely cost range, key assumptions, and major levers before committing to a multi-region rollout of the profile and identity flow.

title: Decide whether to invest in notification preference center for training managers to improve localization success
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether a product team should invest in a notification preference center for training managers who coordinate localized training programs across regions, languages, and business units. These managers often receive notifications about translation readiness, regional reviewer approvals, launch dates, compliance changes, learner communications, and localization defects. Poorly timed, irrelevant, or overly frequent notifications can cause missed actions, delayed launches, and lower confidence in localized training rollouts.

The strategic question is whether building a dedicated preference center is the right investment to improve localization success, compared with alternatives such as better default notification rules, smarter prioritization, regional admin workflows, digest emails, or operational process changes. Your recommendation should consider the size and urgency of the problem, the target users’ decision-making power, product complexity, and whether this capability creates durable value for global training operations.

You should make a clear recommendation on whether to invest now, defer, run a smaller test, or pursue an alternative path. Frame the decision around expected customer impact, business value, implementation cost, risks, and what evidence would be needed to move forward confidently.

The experience should consider:
- The workflow of training managers managing localized content launches, approvals, deadlines, and regional communications
- The specific notification pain points that may affect localization success, such as missed deadlines, alert fatigue, wrong-language messages, or timezone issues
- Strategic options beyond a full preference center, including better defaults, role-based notification logic, digests, escalation rules, or regional templates
- The right to win: whether this product is best positioned to solve the problem through data, workflow ownership, customer trust, or global scale
- Trade-offs between user control, product complexity, operational support, and consistency of critical communications
- Risks such as users disabling important alerts, fragmented notification behavior, accessibility gaps, or added administrative burden
- Decision gates and success signals, such as evidence of notification-related launch delays, manager adoption, reduced missed actions, and improved localized rollout quality

Your goal is to provide a structured strategy recommendation that connects user pain to business outcome, compares realistic investment paths, and defines what the team should do next without jumping directly into feature design.

title: A competitor is attacking marketplace checkout and product discovery. What should Ecommerce do next under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints?
description:
Problem Statement Description

Ecommerce is facing a competitive threat from a rival marketplace that is improving two high-leverage parts of the buyer journey: product discovery and checkout. The concern is especially acute for first-time buyers, who may have low trust, limited purchase history, and higher sensitivity to search relevance, seller credibility, payment reliability, delivery promises, and return policies.

You are asked to define what Ecommerce should do next as a product strategy leader. The decision should account for marketplace scale, the incentives of sellers and buyers, catalog quality, privacy and data limitations, accessibility, operational cost, and regulatory constraints that may affect ranking, personalization, payments, data use, and marketplace fairness.

This is not a feature-design exercise alone. Frame the strategic options available, identify where Ecommerce has a right to win, and explain how you would decide between competing investments across discovery, checkout, trust, seller quality, and operational levers.

The experience should consider:
- The specific first-time buyer journey from landing, searching or browsing, evaluating products, adding to cart, paying, and completing the order.
- Competitive attack vectors in discovery and checkout, including relevance, speed, trust, personalization, payments, guarantees, and post-purchase confidence.
- Strategic options, trade-offs, and sequencing across short-term conversion gains and longer-term marketplace health.
- Seller incentives, catalog accuracy, fulfillment promises, returns, and how changes may affect seller behavior.
- Privacy, data quality, responsible AI, accessibility, and regulatory risks in ranking, recommendations, and checkout flows.
- Cost, operational load, fraud risk, payment reliability, and global scale considerations.
- Decision gates and success signals that would indicate whether to double down, pivot, or stop an initiative.

The goal is to present a clear strategic recommendation for Ecommerce’s next move, supported by market reasoning, customer insight, business impact, constraints, risks, and a practical path to validate the direction without overcommitting prematurely.

title: Root cause a sudden decline in retention among sales teams using Jobs at global scale
description:
About LinkedIn
LinkedIn is a professional networking platform that connects individuals and businesses for career development and opportunities.

Context
LinkedIn Jobs has experienced a sudden decline in retention among global sales teams. This issue affects users who rely on the platform for hiring and recruiting activities.

Key details
- Product: LinkedIn Jobs
- Situation: sudden decline in retention
- Scope: The drop started within the last 7 days

How you'll be evaluated
Structured diagnosis · Hypothesis prioritization · Data validation · Fix and prevention

title: Tell me about a time you handled a difficult stakeholder while protecting successful application completion under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to describe a real situation where you managed a difficult stakeholder in a government digital service context while still protecting citizen outcomes. The scenario should involve citizens applying for benefits through an application process where completion mattered, such as eligibility submission, identity verification, document upload, case review, or assisted-channel support.

Your story should show how you balanced stakeholder pressure with public-service obligations: regulatory compliance, fraud prevention, privacy, accessibility, inclusion, operational capacity, and fairness. The “difficult stakeholder” could be a policy owner, legal/compliance partner, operations lead, engineering lead, executive sponsor, vendor, or regional service owner whose goals or constraints created tension with successful application completion at scale.

Focus on the evidence of your product leadership: how you understood the stakeholder’s incentives, clarified the user and business impact, aligned teams around trade-offs, and protected the integrity of the application journey without bypassing required controls. The strongest examples will show measurable citizen impact, responsible decision-making, and reflection on what you would repeat or change.

The experience should consider:

- The specific application workflow and where completion was at risk, such as account creation, eligibility checks, identity proofing, document submission, appointment scheduling, or final confirmation.
- The stakeholder conflict: what the stakeholder wanted, why it was difficult, and how their incentives differed from citizen needs, operational realities, or regulatory obligations.
- The scale and sensitivity of the environment, including high application volume, vulnerable users, multilingual needs, accessibility requirements, or assisted service centers.
- The constraints you had to respect, such as data privacy, auditability, fraud controls, procurement/vendor limits, legacy systems, policy rules, or legal deadlines.
- The actions you personally took to diagnose the issue, create alignment, influence without authority, escalate appropriately, or negotiate trade-offs.
- The outcome, including impact on successful application completion, error rates, processing time, call-center load, compliance risk, stakeholder trust, or citizen satisfaction.
- What you learned about managing complex public-sector stakeholders while maintaining trust, fairness, and service reliability.

Your goal is to tell a structured, credible story that demonstrates ownership, judgment, resilience, and stakeholder management in a high-stakes government product environment where user completion, public accountability, and regulatory discipline all mattered.

title: Evaluate the technical trade-offs of adding AI to fraud detection workflow
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether and how to add AI capabilities to an existing fraud detection workflow for a large-scale consumer product used by families. The current system may include rules, risk thresholds, manual review queues, account verification, payment checks, device signals, and user appeals. The business goal is risk reduction, but the product must also preserve trust for parents, guardians, and family members who may share devices, payment methods, addresses, or accounts.

The core challenge is to assess the technical trade-offs of introducing AI into this workflow without assuming that “more AI” is automatically better. You should consider where AI could fit, such as risk scoring, anomaly detection, identity verification support, review prioritization, case summarization, or investigator assistance, and what new risks this creates around accuracy, latency, explainability, bias, privacy, security, and operational dependency.

This is a Technical PM problem. Focus on product requirements, system architecture implications, data needs, model lifecycle, APIs, reliability, observability, rollout strategy, and cross-functional trade-offs between fraud prevention, user experience, compliance, and operational efficiency.

The experience should consider:
- The end-to-end fraud workflow, including detection, decisioning, user friction, manual review, appeals, and resolution.
- Family-specific patterns such as shared devices, child accounts, guardian approvals, joint payment instruments, and legitimate behavior that may look suspicious.
- Data requirements, including event streams, transaction history, account relationships, device signals, labels, feedback loops, and data quality constraints.
- Technical integration points between AI models, rules engines, risk services, case management tools, customer support systems, and user-facing verification flows.
- Reliability and performance expectations, including latency, uptime, fallback behavior, model drift, and graceful degradation if AI services fail.
- Privacy, security, consent, retention, and access-control implications when using sensitive family, payment, identity, or behavioral data.
- Explainability, auditability, fairness, and compliance needs for decisions that may block accounts, transactions, or family access.
- Rollout, experimentation, monitoring, incident response, and human-in-the-loop controls to manage false positives, false negatives, and operational load.

Your goal is to frame a balanced technical evaluation: define what problem AI is meant to solve, what requirements and constraints matter, what trade-offs must be made, and how the organization should decide whether the AI-enhanced workflow is safe, useful, and scalable enough to pursue.

title: Design a fraud alert experience for review operations teams that improves support deflection
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are designing a fraud alert experience for review operations teams working inside a large-scale digital platform such as a marketplace, fintech product, SaaS admin system, or consumer account ecosystem. These teams review suspicious activity, validate fraud signals, resolve escalations, and help prevent unnecessary support contacts from customers, merchants, internal agents, or account owners who are confused by holds, blocks, warnings, or verification requests.

Today, fraud-related alerts can create operational friction: reviewers may see incomplete context, duplicate alerts, unclear severity, inconsistent next steps, or limited visibility into whether an issue is already being handled. As a result, legitimate users may contact support for status updates, frontline agents may escalate cases unnecessarily, and review teams may spend time answering avoidable questions instead of resolving high-risk fraud events.

Design the product experience that review operations teams would use to understand, prioritize, investigate, act on, and communicate about fraud alerts in a way that reduces avoidable support demand while preserving trust, safety, accuracy, and fairness. Focus on the reviewer workflow and the surrounding handoffs rather than only the end-user notification.

The experience should consider:
- Who the primary and secondary users are, including fraud reviewers, review leads, support agents, risk policy teams, and affected customers or merchants.
- The end-to-end workflow from fraud signal generation to alert triage, investigation, decisioning, communication, and case closure.
- The key pain points that cause support contacts, such as unclear status, missing evidence, repeated verification requests, delayed decisions, or inconsistent messaging.
- How reviewers should see alert severity, confidence, reason codes, user history, prior actions, and recommended next steps without creating cognitive overload.
- How the system should support collaboration, escalation, auditability, and handoffs between fraud operations and customer support.
- How to balance support deflection with user trust, false-positive risk, privacy, accessibility, compliance, and responsible use of automation.
- What success would look like across operational efficiency, support contact reduction, reviewer productivity, resolution quality, and customer outcomes.

Your goal is to frame a clear product design approach for a fraud alert experience that helps operations teams resolve fraud cases more effectively and proactively prevents unnecessary support interactions, while ensuring that legitimate users are treated fairly and high-risk activity is handled safely.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling field service routing for retail staff
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale a field service routing product used by retail staff, where the immediate product goal is activation: getting store associates, managers, or field reps to successfully complete their first meaningful routed visit, task, or service workflow. The system may need to assign routes, sequence locations, account for staff availability, handle store operating constraints, and adapt to real-world changes such as delays, cancellations, traffic, or inventory/service readiness.

The challenge is not only to design routing logic, but to reason through the technical trade-offs required as usage grows across many stores, regions, roles, and operational patterns. You should consider how the product experience supports a new retail staff member from onboarding through first route acceptance and completion, while balancing routing quality, latency, reliability, data accuracy, privacy, and operational complexity.

Assume stakeholders include retail staff in the field, store managers, regional operations teams, customer support, data science/optimization teams, and platform engineering. The interview is focused on your ability as a Technical PM to frame requirements, evaluate architecture and API/data implications, make trade-offs explicit, and connect technical decisions back to activation outcomes.

The experience should consider:
- Core user workflows for retail staff activation, including onboarding, route assignment, task understanding, navigation, completion, and exception handling.
- Functional and non-functional requirements for routing at scale, such as latency, throughput, route freshness, availability, offline tolerance, and accuracy.
- Data inputs and integrations, including staff schedules, store locations, task priority, service windows, inventory or readiness signals, traffic/location data, and completion events.
- Trade-offs between real-time optimization, batch routing, rule-based assignment, heuristic approaches, and more advanced optimization or AI-driven methods.
- API and system design considerations, including route generation, route updates, mobile client sync, event ingestion, permissions, and auditability.
- Privacy, security, and trust implications around employee location, performance data, access control, and data retention.
- Rollout and observability needs, including instrumentation for activation, route acceptance, completion, latency, failures, override rates, and operational escalations.
- Product trade-offs between routing efficiency, staff autonomy, manager control, fairness, explainability, and ease of adoption.

Your goal is to evaluate the technical options and constraints clearly enough to recommend how the team should reason about scaling the routing system while improving activation, without jumping directly to a single implementation.

title: Create a metric tree for repeat group orders in food-delivery
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are a PM working on Swiggy’s group ordering experience for office lunches in urban India. The target user is typically an office lunch coordinator who starts or manages a shared order for a team, gets colleagues to participate, handles timing and preferences, and expects the order to arrive reliably during a limited lunch window.

The interview task is to create a metric tree for repeat group orders. The focus is not just on whether a group order happened once, but whether the same coordinator, team, workplace, or participant group comes back to use the experience again. Your metric structure should help Swiggy understand what drives repeat behavior and where the funnel or experience may be breaking down.

The metric tree should account for the realities of food delivery: restaurant availability, prep-time variability, delivery batching, payment coordination, cancellations, substitutions, late participants, and trust in delivery accuracy. It should also be useful for product decisions, experimentation, and operational diagnosis rather than being a list of disconnected numbers.

The experience should consider:
- How to define a “repeat group order” clearly, including the actor, time window, and denominator.
- Whether repeat behavior should be measured at coordinator, office, group, participant, or restaurant level.
- The full group-order workflow: creation, invite sharing, participant joining, cart building, payment, checkout, delivery, and post-order satisfaction.
- Instrumentation needed to distinguish individual orders from true group orders and to capture drop-offs accurately.
- Cohorts such as new vs returning coordinators, office size, weekday lunch patterns, city, restaurant type, and delivery distance.
- Guardrail metrics around delivery reliability, cancellation, refunds, customer support contacts, restaurant load, and delivery partner efficiency.
- Data quality, privacy, and consent considerations when associating users with workplaces or recurring groups.
- How the metric tree would help diagnose whether repeat orders are limited by demand, product friction, supply availability, or operational reliability.

The goal is to define a clear, decision-useful metric hierarchy that connects the business outcome of repeat group orders to measurable user behaviors, funnel steps, quality signals, and operational constraints in Swiggy’s food-delivery marketplace.

title: Define success metrics for B2B onboarding console serving remote teams
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a B2B onboarding console used by remote teams to set up their organization, invite members, configure permissions, connect tools, complete compliance steps, and reach a productive first-use state without heavy support involvement. The business priority is cost efficiency, so the metric framework should help determine whether onboarding is becoming less expensive to deliver while still producing successful, trustworthy customer outcomes.

This is a metrics interview question. Focus on defining what “success” means for a remote-team onboarding workflow, how you would measure it end-to-end, and how those measures would inform product and operational decisions. Consider that remote teams may have distributed admins, asynchronous collaboration, multiple approval steps, different time zones, and varying technical maturity.

Your scope should include both customer-facing onboarding outcomes and internal cost drivers, such as support burden, implementation effort, automation quality, failed setup recovery, and time-to-value. Avoid treating cost reduction in isolation; the metrics should make it clear when efficiency gains are creating hidden risks such as poor activation, lower customer trust, increased churn, or unresolved setup issues.

The experience should consider:
- Clear definitions for onboarding start, completion, activation, and “ready for productive use”
- Denominators for each metric, including eligible accounts, invited users, admins, and completed setup flows
- Instrumentation across console events, support contacts, admin actions, integrations, permissions, and handoff points
- Cohorts by company size, remote-team maturity, region, plan type, integration complexity, and onboarding path
- Cost-efficiency measures that distinguish automation savings from deferred or shifted customer effort
- Guardrails for customer satisfaction, trust, security/compliance completion, accessibility, reliability, and retention
- Leading indicators that help teams intervene before expensive support escalations or failed onboarding
- Decision usefulness for product, customer success, implementation, and finance teams

The goal is to produce a practical metrics framework that can guide whether the onboarding console is improving operational leverage for B2B remote teams while preserving a high-quality onboarding experience and long-term customer value.

title: Estimate the operational cost of scaling fraud detection workflow to multiple regions
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are estimating the annual operational cost of expanding a fraud detection workflow from one region to multiple regions for a large-scale consumer technology product used by families. The workflow may include automated risk scoring, manual review, user appeals, regional policy tuning, customer support handoffs, compliance processes, and monitoring of fraud patterns that differ by geography.

The estimate should focus on operational costs required to run and scale the workflow, not the business case or product strategy. Consider how family accounts may create unique fraud and safety scenarios, such as shared devices, child or guardian account controls, payment misuse, account takeover, fake identity patterns, and false positives that can disrupt legitimate household usage.

You should define the scope clearly: which regions are included, what “fraud detection workflow” covers, what cost categories are in or out, and whether you are estimating monthly, quarterly, or annual cost. Your answer should make assumptions explicit, use a structured breakdown, and show how the estimate changes under different scale or risk conditions.

The experience should consider:
- The unit of estimation, such as cost per region, cost per active family account, cost per flagged event, or cost per manual review.
- The target population and transaction/activity volume across regions.
- Expected fraud alert rates, review rates, appeal rates, and repeat-case frequency.
- Operational staffing needs, including fraud analysts, quality assurance, policy operations, localization, compliance, and support escalation.
- Tooling and infrastructure costs, such as case management systems, model monitoring, data pipelines, vendor tools, and regional reporting.
- Regional cost differences, including labor rates, language coverage, local regulations, and time-zone requirements.
- Key assumptions and sensitivity drivers, such as fraud prevalence, automation accuracy, false-positive rate, and review handling time.
- Sanity checks against comparable support, trust-and-safety, or risk operations benchmarks.

Your goal is to produce a defensible, structured guesstimate that helps leadership understand the likely operational investment needed to scale fraud detection across regions, the biggest cost drivers, and where uncertainty could materially change the estimate.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in risk reduction for payments dispute center
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are investigating an unexpected decline in risk reduction for training managers who use a payments dispute center. The product helps training managers monitor, coach, and improve teams handling payment disputes, chargebacks, fraud signals, policy exceptions, and customer-impacting resolution workflows.

Recently, the measured risk reduction outcome for this segment dropped sharply. Before proposing any fixes, you need to diagnose whether the decline reflects a real deterioration in dispute-handling effectiveness, a change in user behavior, a reporting or instrumentation issue, a shift in case mix, or an operational change affecting training managers and their teams.

Frame the investigation as an RCA for a payments and risk product where trust, compliance, financial exposure, and operational accuracy matter. Focus on how you would isolate the anomaly, validate the metric, segment the issue, and gather evidence before deciding what action is appropriate.

The experience should consider:
- How “risk reduction” is defined, measured, and attributed to training manager activity
- Whether the drop is sudden, gradual, localized, or tied to a specific release, workflow, region, dispute type, or team
- Instrumentation checks across dashboards, event tracking, data pipelines, metric logic, and denominator changes
- Segmentation by training manager cohort, agent team, payment method, dispute category, geography, merchant type, and case severity
- Behavioral signals such as training completion, coaching activity, review quality, escalation rates, and tool usage frequency
- External or operational factors such as policy changes, fraud pattern shifts, staffing changes, backlog spikes, or new dispute rules
- Evidence needed to distinguish metric noise from a real increase in risk exposure
- Short-term containment, stakeholder communication, and prevention mechanisms once the root cause is confirmed

The goal is to demonstrate a structured RCA approach that protects payment integrity and customer trust while avoiding premature conclusions. Your diagnosis should show how you would move from anomaly detection to validated root cause using data, segmentation, product understanding, and operational context.

title: Define success metrics for usage-based billing console serving support agents
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a usage-based billing console used by support agents who help customers understand invoices, investigate usage spikes, resolve billing disputes, and decide what guidance or next action to provide. The console surfaces recommendations to agents, such as likely causes of a charge, relevant usage events, plan or quota information, policy guidance, escalation paths, credits, or customer-facing explanations.

The primary business goal is recommendation relevance: whether the console provides the right recommendation for the customer’s billing context at the moment the agent needs it. This is a high-stakes workflow because incorrect or poorly timed recommendations can increase handle time, create customer distrust, trigger unnecessary credits or escalations, and expose sensitive billing or usage data.

Define a metrics framework that would allow the product team to evaluate whether the console is succeeding for agents, customers, and the business. Your answer should make clear how you would measure relevance, how you would instrument the workflow, and how you would distinguish recommendation quality from broader support operations outcomes.

The experience should consider:
- The agent workflow from case intake, account and usage review, recommendation viewing, action selection, customer response, and case resolution.
- Clear definitions for recommendation impressions, eligible cases, accepted recommendations, ignored recommendations, overrides, escalations, and resolved cases.
- How relevance should be measured, including denominator choices and whether metrics are case-level, recommendation-level, agent-level, or customer-level.
- Instrumentation needed to capture agent actions, recommendation ranking, context shown, timestamps, edits, downstream outcomes, and feedback signals.
- Cohorts such as new versus experienced agents, billing issue type, customer segment, product line, geography, usage volume, and recommendation category.
- Guardrail metrics for billing accuracy, customer trust, privacy/security, support quality, handle time, escalation rate, credit leakage, and agent overreliance.
- How metrics would be used for decision-making, experimentation, model or rules tuning, rollout readiness, and ongoing monitoring.

The goal is to define a practical, decision-useful measurement approach for a support-agent billing console where recommendation relevance is the central outcome, while ensuring the metrics account for operational realities, customer impact, and risks inherent in usage-based billing support.

title: Design an experimentation dashboard for Stock
description:
About Adobe
Adobe provides software solutions for creative professionals and businesses to create, manage, and deliver digital content.

Context
Adobe Stock provides small businesses with access to creative assets for marketing. Product teams need a dashboard to monitor and analyze experimentation outcomes effectively.

Key details
- Users: small businesses
- Product: Adobe Stock
- Situation: experimentation dashboard design
- Goal: enable disciplined experimentation and reliable product decisions

Key terms
- A/B tests: Experiments comparing two versions to determine which performs better

How you'll be evaluated
Goal clarity · Metric selection · Trade-offs and guardrails · Measurement plan

title: Prioritize the next strategic bet in fraud detection workflow under constrained investment
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the next major strategic investment for a fraud detection workflow serving families in a large-scale consumer or platform product. Families may include parents, children, caregivers, shared accounts, shared payment instruments, family plans, or household-level permissions, creating fraud patterns that differ from individual users. The business outcome is risk reduction, but the investment budget, engineering capacity, operational bandwidth, and compliance tolerance are constrained.

The current workflow likely spans fraud signal collection, automated detection, risk scoring, user verification, case review, appeals, and post-incident recovery. Key pain points may include account takeover, scams targeting vulnerable family members, unauthorized purchases, synthetic or shared-identity abuse, false positives that block legitimate family activity, and manual review queues that do not scale globally.

Your task is to prioritize the next strategic bet, not to design a single feature in isolation. You should frame the decision among plausible investment options, explain trade-offs, identify the company’s right to win, define what evidence would change the decision, and show how you would manage risk before committing significant resources.

Your strategy should consider:
- The highest-risk fraud scenarios for families and how they differ from individual-user fraud patterns
- The strategic options available, such as prevention, detection, user education, recovery, workflow automation, or third-party partnerships
- Expected impact on fraud loss, customer trust, operational cost, user friction, and accessibility
- Trade-offs between aggressive risk controls and false positives that may harm legitimate family usage
- Data, AI, privacy, compliance, and responsible-use constraints, especially for minors or vulnerable users
- Market and platform dynamics, including global scale, local fraud patterns, and regulatory variation
- Decision gates, pilot criteria, investment sizing, and signals that would justify scaling or stopping
- Key risks, dependencies, and mitigations across product, operations, legal, policy, and engineering teams

The goal is to present a clear strategic recommendation framework for choosing the next fraud-detection workflow bet under constrained investment, with a defensible rationale for prioritization, explicit trade-offs, and a path to validate whether the bet materially reduces risk while preserving family trust.

title: Tell me about leading ambiguous work related to AI meeting assistant
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to describe a real situation where you led work with unclear scope, shifting requirements, or uncertain user expectations in the context of an AI meeting assistant for premium subscribers. The interviewer is looking for evidence that you can create clarity, make sound product judgments, and build trust when the product involves AI-generated outputs such as summaries, action items, transcripts, recommendations, or meeting follow-ups.

Your story should be grounded in a premium subscriber experience where trust was especially important: users may be paying for higher accuracy, privacy, reliability, control, and workflow integration. The ambiguity could have come from unclear customer needs, technical limitations, legal or privacy concerns, model quality issues, stakeholder disagreement, or uncertainty about how users would adopt AI assistance in sensitive meeting contexts.

Focus on your personal ownership: how you framed the problem, aligned stakeholders, made trade-offs, validated user trust, and drove progress despite incomplete information. The strongest responses will show how you balanced user value, responsible AI behavior, business impact, and execution discipline.

The experience should consider:
- What made the work ambiguous and why it mattered for premium subscribers.
- The specific AI meeting assistant workflow involved, such as recording consent, transcription, summarization, action-item extraction, sharing, search, or integrations.
- How you identified trust risks, including accuracy, hallucinations, privacy, permissions, data retention, transparency, or user control.
- How you brought structure to the problem through customer research, data, experiments, stakeholder alignment, or phased decision-making.
- The role you personally played versus engineering, design, data science, legal, customer support, or go-to-market teams.
- The trade-offs you made between speed, model quality, user experience, compliance, and subscriber expectations.
- The measurable or observable impact on trust, adoption, retention, support burden, satisfaction, or product quality.
- What you learned and how it changed your approach to leading AI product work.

The goal is to tell a concise, credible leadership story that demonstrates ownership in uncertainty, strong product judgment, responsible AI thinking, and the ability to earn user trust in a premium AI-powered experience.

title: Estimate revenue upside if perfect order rate improves by 10% for premium quick-commerce users under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints
description:
Problem Statement Description

Blinkit wants to understand the revenue upside from improving the “perfect order rate” by 10% for its premium quick-commerce users. A perfect order can be interpreted as an order that is delivered on time, fully fulfilled, with accurate items, acceptable substitutions where needed, and no refund, complaint, or support escalation.

This is a guesstimate question set in a high-scale instant grocery environment, where premium users place frequent, high-expectation orders and are sensitive to delays, stockouts, poor substitutions, and service failures. The estimate should account for how better order quality may affect repeat purchase frequency, retention, basket size, refunds, incentives, and trust.

Your task is not to propose a product solution, but to size the potential revenue upside using clear assumptions. You should define the scope, identify the relevant user and order base, estimate current performance, and reason through how a 10% improvement in perfect order rate translates into incremental revenue under operational, incentive, and regulatory constraints.

The experience should consider:
- The definition of “premium quick-commerce users” and whether the estimate is city-level, national, monthly, quarterly, or annual.
- The unit of analysis: users, orders, gross order value, net revenue, contribution margin, or another revenue proxy.
- Current order volume, order frequency, average order value, and baseline perfect order rate assumptions.
- How imperfect orders currently impact refunds, cancellations, credits, churn, reduced frequency, and customer support costs.
- Whether the 10% improvement is relative or absolute, and how that changes the calculation.
- Adoption and behavior change assumptions, including how many affected users would order more often or stay longer.
- Constraints such as dark-store inventory accuracy, picker capacity, delivery SLA pressure, incentive costs, privacy/data quality, and regulatory limits.
- Sensitivity checks for best-case, base-case, and conservative scenarios.

The goal is to produce a structured, defensible revenue upside estimate with transparent assumptions, clear denominators, and sanity checks. A strong answer should show how operational quality improvements connect to customer behavior and business outcomes without overclaiming precision.

title: Prioritize a quarterly roadmap for Uber Eats
description:
About Uber
Uber provides a platform for ride-hailing and food delivery services.

Context
Uber Eats is focusing on food delivery for airport travelers. Enhancements are needed for user experience and operational efficiency in time-sensitive situations.

Key details
- Users: airport travelers
- Product: Uber Eats
- Situation: quarterly roadmap prioritization
- Goal: improve food delivery for travelers

Key terms
- marketplace liquidity: the availability of goods and services in a marketplace

title: Stock accuracy dropped suddenly in inventory management. Diagnose the root cause
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are investigating a sudden drop in stock accuracy for an inventory management product used by premium subscribers. These customers rely on the system to keep on-hand, reserved, in-transit, and available-to-sell quantities aligned with warehouse, POS, marketplace, and order-management activity. A sudden accuracy decline can create overselling, stockouts, unnecessary replenishment, fulfillment delays, and loss of trust among high-value customers.

Your task is to diagnose the root cause of the anomaly as a product manager. Treat this as a real production incident: first clarify what “stock accuracy” means, confirm whether the drop is real or measurement-related, identify affected customer segments, workflows, integrations, SKUs, locations, and time windows, then form and test hypotheses using product, operational, and system evidence.

The investigation should account for the fact that premium subscribers may use more advanced capabilities, such as multi-location inventory, automated syncs, bulk imports, forecasting, barcode workflows, API integrations, reserved inventory, or priority support. The issue may come from user behavior, process gaps, integration failures, data latency, recent product changes, or instrumentation problems, so the diagnosis should separate symptom from cause.

The experience should consider:
- How stock accuracy is defined, including numerator, denominator, expected reconciliation source, and acceptable variance.
- Whether the decline is global or concentrated by subscriber tier, warehouse, region, SKU category, integration partner, device type, workflow, or account cohort.
- Instrumentation checks for metric pipeline changes, event loss, duplicate updates, delayed syncs, schema changes, or reporting lag.
- Recent launches, configuration changes, API updates, import tools, automation rules, permission changes, or operational process changes that could affect inventory counts.
- User workflow points where inventory can diverge, such as receiving, picking, returns, cancellations, transfers, manual adjustments, reservations, and cycle counts.
- Evidence needed to validate or reject hypotheses, including logs, audit trails, support tickets, reconciliation reports, customer interviews, and experiment or rollout timelines.
- Immediate mitigation options for affected customers, including communication, manual reconciliation, feature rollback, sync replay, alerts, or temporary safeguards.
- Longer-term prevention through monitoring, anomaly detection, data quality checks, user education, integration SLAs, and incident review.

The goal is to demonstrate a structured RCA approach that narrows a broad stock accuracy drop into a defensible root cause or set of causes, prioritizes customer impact for premium subscribers, and defines what evidence, mitigations, and prevention mechanisms would be needed before declaring the incident resolved.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in recommendation relevance for offline order capture
description:
Problem Statement Description

Agency owners rely on an offline order capture workflow to record orders when connectivity is limited, sales happen in the field, or orders are entered in batches after customer interactions. Within that workflow, the product surfaces recommendations—such as suggested products, quantities, customer-specific items, replenishment questions, pricing-related suggestions, or next-best actions—to help agencies capture accurate orders faster.

A sudden drop has been observed in recommendation relevance specifically for agency owners using offline order capture. The issue may be visible through lower acceptance of recommendations, more manual overrides, complaints about poor suggestions, reduced order completion efficiency, or downstream order quality problems. Your task is to diagnose what may have changed before proposing any fixes.

Assume this is a live production issue in a scaled product environment where recommendations depend on user behavior, catalog data, customer history, availability, pricing, sync behavior, and offline-to-online data reconciliation. You should frame the incident clearly, identify where the drop is happening, validate whether the metric reflects real user pain, and reason through likely product, data, model, infrastructure, and workflow causes.

The experience should consider:

- How to define “recommendation relevance” for offline order capture, including acceptance rate, edit rate, dismissal rate, reorder accuracy, conversion, time-to-capture, and qualitative feedback.
- Which agency-owner cohorts, geographies, catalog categories, device types, app versions, connectivity states, and order-entry modes are affected.
- Whether the anomaly is real or caused by instrumentation, logging gaps, delayed syncs, metric denominator changes, attribution issues, or dashboard pipeline problems.
- What recent changes may have impacted the workflow, such as recommendation model updates, catalog refreshes, pricing changes, inventory constraints, UI changes, offline cache logic, or sync behavior.
- How offline-specific constraints could distort recommendations, including stale local data, incomplete customer history, failed background syncs, conflict resolution, and delayed availability updates.
- How to separate user-behavior changes from system-caused degradation, including seasonality, agency workload shifts, promotion changes, customer mix changes, or supply constraints.
- What evidence would be needed to prioritize hypotheses, such as event logs, model inputs and outputs, before/after comparisons, user sessions, support tickets, and sample order traces.
- How to think about immediate mitigation, user communication, monitoring, and prevention without jumping prematurely to a fix.

Your goal is to walk through a structured root-cause analysis that narrows the problem from a broad relevance drop to the most plausible causes, using segmentation, instrumentation checks, hypothesis testing, and evidence-based reasoning before recommending next steps.

title: Design the technical product architecture for support automation at large scale
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are designing the technical product architecture for a support automation platform serving creators at large scale. Creators may contact support for account access, monetization issues, content policy appeals, payout delays, feature bugs, safety concerns, or platform guidance, and they expect fast, accurate, and trustworthy resolution without repeatedly explaining their context.

The current support experience may involve fragmented help-center content, manual triage, long queues, inconsistent agent responses, limited visibility into ticket status, and difficulty escalating urgent or sensitive cases. The product must improve resolution speed while preserving quality, fairness, privacy, and user trust across languages, geographies, creator tiers, and issue types.

As a Technical PM, your task is to describe the architecture and product requirements for an automated support system that can ingest creator requests, classify intent, retrieve relevant context, automate safe resolutions where appropriate, route complex cases to human agents, and continuously learn from outcomes. The scope should include both creator-facing and internal support workflows, not just a chatbot interface.

The experience should consider:
- Creator entry points, authentication, account context, ticket creation, status tracking, and escalation paths
- Data sources such as help content, account metadata, policy systems, transaction records, moderation history, and prior support interactions
- APIs, event flows, permissioning, audit logs, and integrations with CRM, workflow, notification, and knowledge-management systems
- AI/automation boundaries, confidence thresholds, human-in-the-loop review, fallback handling, and responsible use of generated responses
- Reliability, latency, availability, disaster recovery, observability, and operational monitoring at global scale
- Privacy, security, access control, regulatory constraints, data retention, and sensitive-case handling
- Rollout strategy, experimentation, localization, accessibility, and support for different creator segments and issue severities
- Product trade-offs between speed, cost, accuracy, personalization, explainability, and risk of incorrect automation

Your goal is to frame a scalable technical architecture and product approach that materially reduces time to resolution for creators while maintaining support quality, compliance, and trust. Focus on requirements, system interactions, data and API design, rollout considerations, and the trade-offs a Technical PM would need to manage.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for field service routing among review operations teams
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are estimating the annual opportunity for a field service routing product used by review operations teams. These teams handle high-volume review workflows such as content, listings, merchant, fraud, trust-and-safety, compliance, or support case reviews, where work must be routed from intake to the right reviewer, specialist queue, escalation path, QA team, or field operations partner.

The core workflow involves receiving review items, classifying urgency and complexity, assigning them based on skills, region, policy expertise, availability, and SLA, then handing off context across teams when additional review or action is needed. Poor routing can create duplicate work, delayed decisions, missed SLAs, inconsistent outcomes, reviewer rework, and low-quality handoffs where critical context is lost.

Your estimate should quantify the annual opportunity size in a clear unit, such as revenue opportunity, cost savings, productivity gain, avoidable rework, or total addressable spend. You should also connect the estimate to handoff quality: how better routing improves the completeness, timeliness, and accuracy of transitions between intake, review, escalation, field action, and QA.

The estimate should consider:
- The scope of review operations included, such as internal review teams, outsourced BPO teams, specialist reviewers, QA teams, and field operations handoff points.
- The relevant population or volume base, such as number of companies, operations teams, reviewers, review cases, handoffs, or routed tasks per year.
- Adoption assumptions, including what share of teams would need routing support and how frequently routing or handoffs occur.
- The unit economics of the workflow, including reviewer cost, case handling time, escalation cost, rework rate, SLA penalties, or quality-related business impact.
- How handoff quality is measured, such as missing context rate, reassignment rate, escalation accuracy, time-to-resolution, QA defect rate, or first-touch resolution.
- Key assumptions and sensitivity drivers, especially case volume, percentage of complex cases, number of handoffs per case, routing error rate, and value per avoided defect.
- Sanity checks against operational reality, such as reviewer capacity, queue sizes, labor costs, and whether the resulting opportunity is plausible for large-scale review environments.

The goal is to produce a structured, defensible guesstimate that defines the market or operational opportunity clearly, shows the main assumptions, highlights the biggest drivers of uncertainty, and explains why improving routing and handoff quality could create meaningful annual value for review operations teams.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for developer API portal among team leads
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are asked to estimate the annual opportunity for a developer API portal targeted at engineering team leads. The portal helps team leads and their developers discover internal or external APIs, evaluate documentation and usage limits, request access, monitor consumption, and plan integration work across products or services.

The estimate should focus on team leads as the primary buyer, influencer, or high-value user segment. Their pain points may include unclear API ownership, slow onboarding, duplicated integration work, poor visibility into usage, unreliable documentation, and difficulty forecasting delivery timelines, API demand, or infrastructure needs.

A strong answer should define what “annual opportunity” means before sizing it: for example, annual revenue potential, annual productivity value, annual addressable spend, or annual business impact from improved forecast accuracy. The estimate should explicitly connect portal adoption and usage to forecast accuracy, such as better prediction of API demand, integration timelines, capacity needs, customer delivery dates, or engineering roadmap commitments.

The experience should consider:
- The scope of the market: internal enterprise developer portals, external API platforms, or both
- The unit of analysis: team leads, engineering teams, developers managed, API-consuming teams, or organizations
- The relevant population and segmentation by company size, industry, developer maturity, and API intensity
- Adoption assumptions, including how many team leads would need such a portal and how frequently they would use it
- Willingness to pay or value created per team lead, team, developer, or organization
- How improved API visibility, documentation, and usage analytics could reduce forecast error or planning variance
- Sensitivity of the estimate to assumptions such as team size, number of APIs, integration frequency, and current workflow inefficiency
- Sanity checks against comparable developer tools, internal platform investments, or SaaS spend patterns

Your goal is to produce a clear, defensible sizing model with explicit assumptions, a logical calculation path, and a brief explanation of how the resulting annual opportunity would be useful for product, go-to-market, or investment decisions tied to forecast accuracy.

title: Describe a time you influenced without authority during a high-stakes launch in the context of fraud detection workflow for families
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to share a concrete example from your past experience where you influenced people or teams without having formal authority, specifically in a high-stakes launch environment involving a fraud detection workflow used by or affecting families. The situation should involve meaningful risk: customer trust, financial or account safety, false positives that could disrupt legitimate family activity, false negatives that could expose families to harm, or operational escalation during launch.

Your story should show how you navigated ambiguity, cross-functional disagreement, urgency, and risk trade-offs. Relevant stakeholders may include product, engineering, data science, risk operations, policy, legal, customer support, design, compliance, or leadership. The interviewer is looking for evidence that you could move a complex launch forward while protecting users and the business, even when you did not directly control the teams or decisions involved.

Focus on what you personally did to align stakeholders, clarify the problem, shape the decision process, manage launch risk, and drive toward a responsible outcome. The example should be specific enough to demonstrate judgment in a fraud-sensitive product environment where families may need both protection and a low-friction experience.

The experience should consider:
- The launch context, why it was high-stakes, and what could have gone wrong for families or the business
- The nature of the fraud detection workflow, including who used it and where friction or risk appeared
- The stakeholders you needed to influence and why you lacked formal authority over them
- The disagreement, resistance, or ambiguity you had to overcome
- The actions you took to build alignment, use evidence, escalate appropriately, or reframe trade-offs
- The measurable or observable impact of your influence on launch quality, risk reduction, customer trust, or operational readiness
- What you learned about influencing in environments involving fraud, safety, trust, and cross-functional accountability

The goal is to tell a structured, high-ownership story that demonstrates credible influence, sound product judgment, and maturity under launch pressure. Your answer should make clear not only what happened, but why your actions mattered and how the experience would translate to future product work involving sensitive user trust and risk-reduction systems.

title: Create a launch plan for inventory forecasting panel aimed at agency owners
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are responsible for launching an inventory forecasting panel for agency owners who manage inventory, staffing, or supply allocation across multiple client accounts or locations. The panel is intended to help them anticipate shortages, overstock, demand spikes, and operational disruptions before they become client-impacting incidents.

This is an execution-focused question. Your task is to create a launch plan that turns the product from ready-for-release into a reliable, adopted, supportable capability in the hands of agency owners. The launch should account for the fact that forecasting errors, stale data, missed alerts, or confusing recommendations can create urgent escalations and damage customer trust.

Assume the product includes forecast views, risk indicators, alerts, and operational workflows that agency owners or their teams use to detect and respond to inventory issues. You do not need to design the forecasting model itself, but you should plan how the product is introduced, monitored, supported, and improved under real-world usage.

The experience should consider:
- Target users, pilot segments, and rollout phases for agency owners with varying inventory complexity
- Launch readiness across product, data pipelines, forecasting quality, support, sales/customer success, and operations
- Clear ownership for incident detection, triage, escalation, customer communication, and resolution
- Dependencies such as data freshness, integrations, alerting systems, permissions, training, and documentation
- Go/no-go criteria, launch gates, and thresholds for forecast accuracy, system reliability, and user comprehension
- Rollback or mitigation plans if forecasts are wrong, alerts misfire, data is delayed, or customers lose confidence
- Communication plans for internal teams and external agency owners before, during, and after launch
- Post-launch monitoring, feedback loops, incident reviews, and iteration cadence

Your goal is to present a practical launch plan that balances speed, reliability, and customer trust. The interviewer is looking for how you sequence the launch, manage cross-functional execution, reduce operational risk, and ensure the product improves incident response rather than creating new incidents.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling AI meeting assistant for mobile-first users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale an AI meeting assistant used primarily by mobile-first users who join, record, summarize, and follow up on meetings from phones rather than desktops. The assistant may capture meeting audio, transcribe conversations, extract decisions and action items, and feed signals into systems used for forecasting, such as sales pipelines, project timelines, staffing plans, or customer commitments.

The core product goal is forecast accuracy: the system should help teams make more reliable predictions based on what actually happened in meetings. Your task is to reason through the technical trade-offs involved in scaling this experience, especially where mobile constraints, AI quality, data freshness, latency, reliability, and user trust may affect the usefulness of downstream forecasts.

This is a technical product-management discussion, so focus on framing requirements, system dependencies, data flows, model behavior, and operational risks. You should evaluate trade-offs rather than jump directly to a single architecture or feature answer.

The experience should consider:
- Mobile-first workflow constraints, including battery, bandwidth, background recording limits, noisy environments, and intermittent connectivity.
- Data capture requirements for audio, transcripts, speaker attribution, meeting metadata, CRM or calendar context, and follow-up actions.
- How AI outputs become forecast inputs, including confidence, completeness, freshness, and traceability of extracted signals.
- Trade-offs between on-device, edge, and cloud processing for latency, cost, accuracy, privacy, and reliability.
- Privacy, consent, security, retention, and access-control expectations for sensitive meeting content.
- Observability needs, including transcription quality, extraction accuracy, model drift, failed syncs, latency, and user corrections.
- Rollout and scaling risks across geographies, languages, device types, network conditions, and enterprise compliance requirements.
- Product trade-offs between automation, user review, correction workflows, and trust in forecast-impacting recommendations.

The goal is to assess how you would structure a technical evaluation for scaling this AI meeting assistant so that it remains dependable for mobile-first users while improving the accuracy and trustworthiness of forecasts derived from meeting data.

title: Plan the MVP launch for restaurant discovery and review trust while balancing user trust, growth, and operational load
description:
Problem Statement Description

Zomato wants to launch an MVP that improves restaurant discovery and review trust for urban diners with dietary constraints, such as vegetarian, vegan, Jain, gluten-free, allergy-sensitive, or religious dietary needs. These users often struggle to determine whether a restaurant is truly suitable for them because reviews may be vague, menus may be outdated, sponsored placements may reduce perceived neutrality, and restaurant-provided information may not always be reliable.

You are asked to plan the MVP launch, not design the full product solution. The launch must balance user trust, booking and order conversion, restaurant participation, and the operational load required to verify or maintain trustworthy information. Assume this is a Zomato environment with discovery, reviews, ratings, menus, ads, delivery, and table booking surfaces already in place.

Your plan should define how the MVP is scoped, sequenced, staffed, monitored, and rolled out safely. It should account for dependencies across product, engineering, design, data science, moderation, sales/account management, restaurant operations, customer support, legal/privacy, and marketing.

The launch plan should consider:
- MVP scope: which diner needs, restaurant categories, cities, and discovery surfaces are included first
- Owners and dependencies across product, engineering, data, review moderation, restaurant operations, and go-to-market teams
- Data readiness, review quality, restaurant data freshness, and how trust-related signals will be maintained after launch
- Sequencing of build, internal testing, pilot launch, restaurant onboarding, user rollout, and post-launch iteration
- Go/no-go criteria, including trust signal accuracy, user comprehension, conversion impact, complaint rate, and operational capacity
- Rollback or mitigation plans if users lose trust, restaurants dispute information, abuse increases, or conversion drops
- Communication plans for diners, restaurants, support teams, and internal stakeholders
- Launch risks around sponsored ranking pressure, privacy, accessibility, moderation cost, and scalability

Your goal is to present a practical MVP execution plan that shows how Zomato can launch this trust-focused restaurant discovery experience in a controlled, measurable, and operationally sustainable way while improving confidence for diners with dietary constraints.

title: Design the technical product architecture for developer platform at large scale
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are designing the technical product architecture for a large-scale developer platform that enables external developers and partner teams to integrate with a technology product used heavily by mobile-first users. The platform may include APIs, SDKs, webhooks, documentation, authentication, sandbox environments, analytics, and operational tooling that help developers build reliable integrations across varied devices, networks, regions, and app ecosystems.

The core challenge is to define an architecture that balances developer ease of use with enterprise-grade reliability, security, privacy, scalability, and operational control. Developers should be able to discover capabilities, authenticate safely, test integrations, monitor usage, handle errors, and ship to production without excessive support dependency or unclear failure modes.

Your response should focus on the technical product design and system-level trade-offs rather than only listing features. Consider how the platform supports integration success at scale, including versioning, backward compatibility, rate limits, observability, developer onboarding, abuse prevention, and rollout strategy.

The experience should consider:
- Developer personas and workflows, including first-time integration, testing, production launch, debugging, and ongoing maintenance
- Core platform components such as APIs, SDKs, developer console, documentation, sandbox, webhooks, auth, analytics, and support surfaces
- API and data design choices, including consistency, latency, error handling, pagination, idempotency, versioning, and backward compatibility
- Mobile-first constraints such as intermittent connectivity, device diversity, app store release cycles, performance, and limited client resources
- Security, privacy, permissions, compliance, secrets management, consent, abuse prevention, and tenant isolation
- Reliability and scale requirements, including SLAs, rate limiting, quotas, retries, failover, incident response, and graceful degradation
- Rollout and observability, including instrumentation, logs, dashboards, alerting, developer health metrics, staged launches, and rollback mechanisms

The goal is to present a clear technical product architecture that enables developers to integrate successfully while protecting end users, maintaining trust, and supporting long-term platform growth at global scale.
