title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling seller performance hub for premium subscribers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale a seller performance hub used by premium subscribers on a large marketplace or commerce platform. These sellers rely on the hub to monitor account health, sales performance, inventory issues, advertising efficiency, fulfillment quality, and recommended actions. The product goal is to improve workflow completion: sellers should be able to identify a performance issue, understand its cause, take the right action, and confirm progress without abandoning the flow.

The current experience may involve fragmented dashboards, slow-loading analytics, stale metrics, inconsistent recommendations, complex permissioning across seller teams, and high support dependence for premium accounts. As usage grows, the system must support more sellers, more data sources, more real-time insights, and more personalized workflows while maintaining trust in the numbers and reliability of the experience.

In this technical PM discussion, focus on the trade-offs involved in scaling the hub: what capabilities the platform must support, where architectural or data constraints may appear, and how product decisions affect latency, accuracy, reliability, cost, privacy, and seller usability. Do not assume unlimited engineering capacity; consider phased delivery, dependencies, and operational risks.

The experience should consider:
- Core seller workflows, including performance diagnosis, recommendation review, action execution, and follow-up tracking.
- Data requirements across orders, listings, inventory, ads, fulfillment, returns, customer feedback, policy compliance, and subscription entitlement.
- API and system dependencies, including data freshness, aggregation logic, permissions, and integration with downstream action systems.
- Reliability and latency expectations for premium subscribers, especially during peak sales periods or business-critical incidents.
- Privacy, security, and access controls for seller business data, team roles, account-level insights, and potentially sensitive recommendations.
- Trade-offs between real-time data and batch processing, personalization and explainability, platform flexibility and operational complexity.
- Rollout and migration considerations, including feature flags, beta cohorts, backward compatibility, support readiness, and rollback paths.
- Observability needs such as workflow funnel tracking, data quality alerts, system health metrics, error diagnostics, and seller-impact monitoring.

Your goal is to frame the technical product problem clearly, identify the most important trade-offs, and explain how you would evaluate scaling decisions in a way that improves workflow completion for premium sellers while preserving trust, performance, and long-term platform maintainability.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling payments dispute center for training managers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale a payments dispute center used by training managers who administer paid learning programs, subscriptions, seat purchases, renewals, invoices, and learner access for their organizations. These users need to understand payment disputes, chargebacks, failed renewals, refunds, evidence requests, and resolution status without disrupting training operations or losing confidence in the platform.

The product goal is renewal confidence: training managers should feel that billing issues are transparent, timely, accurate, and controllable enough to continue renewing their contracts or subscriptions. The technical challenge is to support higher dispute volume, more enterprise accounts, multi-region payment flows, role-based workflows, and operational review without creating brittle systems, compliance risk, or confusing user experiences.

Your task is to frame the technical trade-offs involved in scaling this dispute center. Consider what the platform must support across product experience, APIs, data pipelines, dispute lifecycle state management, integrations with payment processors, internal operations, and customer-facing notifications.

The experience should consider:
- Core workflows for training managers, finance admins, support agents, and internal dispute operations teams.
- Data requirements for dispute status, payment history, invoices, learner access impact, evidence, timestamps, and audit trails.
- API and integration trade-offs with payment processors, CRM systems, support tooling, billing systems, and notification services.
- Reliability expectations, including latency, availability, idempotency, retries, consistency, and failure handling during dispute updates.
- Privacy, security, compliance, and permissions for payment data, organization-level access, uploaded evidence, and audit logs.
- Scalability choices around synchronous vs. asynchronous processing, real-time status updates, queueing, caching, and reconciliation jobs.
- Rollout, migration, and backward-compatibility considerations for existing accounts, historical disputes, and support processes.
- Observability needs, including dispute lifecycle metrics, processor error rates, notification delivery, SLA breaches, and renewal-risk signals.

The goal is to evaluate the technical options, constraints, risks, and product trade-offs clearly enough to guide a scalable implementation plan that improves trust and renewal confidence without prematurely prescribing a single solution.

title: Define success metrics for marketplace quality score serving retail staff
description:

The score is intended to help frontline teams understand marketplace standards, identify areas where quality is below expectation, and complete the right learning content so they can improve day-to-day marketplace execution.

The interview asks you to define success metrics for this score, with learning completion as the primary business goal. Treat this as a metrics design problem: clarify what the product is trying to change, who is included in measurement, how completion should be counted, and how the score’s usefulness should be assessed without relying on vanity metrics.

Your answer should cover both the direct learning outcome and the surrounding product/system health needed to trust the quality score. Consider that retail staff may work across stores, shifts, roles, regions, and varying levels of marketplace responsibility, so metric definitions and cohorts matter.

The experience should consider:

The goal is to present a clear metrics framework that lets a product team determine whether the marketplace quality score is helping retail staff complete the right learning in a measurable, trustworthy, and operationally useful way.

title: Build a 12-month growth strategy for team collaboration focused on power users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are defining a 12-month growth strategy for a team collaboration product, with a specific focus on power users: people or teams who rely on the product frequently, use advanced workflows, influence team norms, and may drive adoption across their organizations. The business priority is improving retention by deepening engagement, strengthening switching costs, and helping these users get more value from the product over time.

This is a strategy exercise, not a feature design task. You should frame the market and customer opportunity, identify strategic options, evaluate trade-offs, and propose how the product and go-to-market teams should sequence bets across the next year. Assume the product operates in a competitive collaboration space where users may already rely on chat, documents, project tracking, meetings, AI assistants, integrations, and workflow automation tools.

Your strategy should account for the fact that power users are valuable but not homogeneous. Some may be team admins, project leads, cross-functional operators, engineering managers, customer support leads, or individual contributors who coordinate work across many stakeholders. Their needs may differ from casual users, and a growth strategy focused on them should be careful not to make the product more complex for everyone else.

The strategy should consider:
- Which power-user segments matter most and how you would define, identify, and prioritize them
- The retention problem being solved, including churn risk, engagement depth, expansion potential, and competitive substitution
- Strategic options across product, pricing/package, integrations, onboarding, community, customer success, and lifecycle engagement
- Trade-offs between serving advanced users and maintaining a simple, accessible experience for broader teams
- The product’s right to win in team collaboration, including network effects, workflow lock-in, data/context advantages, ecosystem partnerships, or trust
- A 12-month sequencing plan with major bets, milestones, dependencies, and decision gates
- Risks such as overbuilding niche features, weakening team-wide adoption, privacy/security concerns, or low organizational buyer support
- How success would be measured through retention, activation of advanced workflows, team expansion, engagement quality, and customer health indicators

Your goal is to present a clear, defensible growth strategy that shows where the company should focus, why power users are the right retention lever, what choices should be made over the next 12 months, and how leadership would know whether to continue, adjust, or stop each major initiative.

title: Design a privacy-safe analytics pipeline for actionable cash-flow task completion rate under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints
description:
Problem Statement Description

Intuit is building a small-business cash-flow assistant for first-time business owners who need help understanding upcoming obligations, prioritizing actions, and completing tasks such as sending invoices, following up on overdue payments, setting aside tax reserves, paying bills, or adjusting payroll timing. The product team wants to measure “actionable cash-flow task completion rate” in a way that is trustworthy, privacy-safe, and useful for improving the customer experience.

Your task is to design the analytics pipeline that would capture, process, protect, and report this metric at scale. The pipeline must work in a regulated financial-data environment where customer trust, accuracy, explainability, data minimization, and compliance are critical. It should also account for incentive risks, such as teams optimizing for task completion in ways that may not actually improve a business owner’s financial confidence or cash-flow health.

Assume the assistant may use sensitive business data such as bank transactions, invoices, bills, payroll, tax estimates, and user interactions. The pipeline should support product, analytics, compliance, and operations stakeholders while ensuring that raw sensitive data is not unnecessarily exposed and that metric outputs remain reliable, auditable, and actionable.

The experience should consider:
- How “actionable cash-flow task completion rate” should be defined, including numerator, denominator, eligibility, task lifecycle, and completion validity.
- What events, APIs, data contracts, and consent states must be captured across the user journey.
- How to handle privacy, data minimization, access control, retention, anonymization or aggregation, and regulatory auditability.
- How to maintain data quality across financial integrations, delayed syncs, duplicate events, offline states, and task updates.
- How to segment results by relevant cohorts without exposing sensitive customer or business information.
- What guardrail metrics are needed to detect harmful incentives, low-quality completions, misleading recommendations, or reduced trust.
- How the pipeline should scale for high event volume, near-real-time monitoring, cost control, reliability, and observability.
- How rollout, experimentation, incident response, and stakeholder reporting should work in a compliance-sensitive environment.

Your goal is to frame a technically credible analytics pipeline and product measurement approach that enables Intuit teams to learn whether cash-flow tasks are being completed in a meaningful, safe, and customer-beneficial way—without compromising privacy, trust, or regulatory obligations.

title: Build a 12-month growth strategy for AI writing assistant focused on first-time buyers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are asked to build a 12-month growth strategy for an AI writing assistant targeting first-time buyers: users or teams who have not previously paid for an AI writing product and may still be uncertain about quality, trust, pricing, and day-to-day usefulness. The product helps users create or improve written content such as emails, documents, marketing copy, proposals, academic drafts, or professional communication.

The strategy should focus on how to grow paid adoption while ensuring users experience high-quality output early enough to justify purchase. First-time buyers may need education, proof of value, confidence in responsible AI use, and a clear path from trial or exploration to paid commitment.

Frame the market opportunity, identify the most attractive buyer segments, and evaluate growth options across acquisition, activation, conversion, retention, partnerships, pricing, and product-led growth. Your answer should make clear trade-offs, sequencing, risks, and how you would decide whether to continue, scale, or change direction during the 12-month period.

The experience should consider:
- Which first-time buyer segments to prioritize and why, such as students, freelancers, small businesses, professionals, creators, or teams
- The main barriers to purchase, including output quality concerns, trust, originality, privacy, cost, workflow fit, and perceived complexity

- Key risks such as low retention, poor output quality, misuse, commoditization, high acquisition cost, or weak differentiation
- Decision gates, leading indicators, and milestones across the 12-month plan

The goal is to present a clear, practical growth strategy that shows where you would focus, what options you would reject or defer, how the company can earn the right to win with first-time buyers, and how success would be evaluated over the year.

title: Evaluate the technical trade-offs of adding AI to subscription billing
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether and how to introduce AI into a subscription billing system used by students, with the business goal of improving revenue recovery from failed payments, expired cards, missed renewals, billing confusion, and involuntary churn. The current billing workflow likely includes plan selection, student eligibility or discount handling, recurring charges, payment retries, invoices/receipts, cancellation flows, customer support escalation, and account access decisions after non-payment.

The interview is not asking you to design a full AI feature in detail or choose a vendor immediately. It is asking you to assess the technical product trade-offs: where AI could add value in the billing lifecycle, what data and system dependencies are required, how reliability and user trust should be protected, and what risks emerge when automated decisions affect student access, payments, or account status.

Because the user segment is students, the experience must account for constrained budgets, irregular cash flow, shared or family payment methods, school calendars, discount eligibility, accessibility needs, and high sensitivity to unexpected charges or loss of access. The billing system also needs to operate at scale, integrate with payment processors and subscription ledgers, and comply with privacy, security, and responsible AI expectations.

The experience should consider:
- Which billing moments AI may influence, such as failed-payment prediction, retry timing, personalized dunning messages, support triage, invoice explanation, fraud/risk review, or churn-risk detection.
- What user, billing, payment, entitlement, support, and communication data would be needed, and whether that data is accurate, timely, consented, and appropriate to use.
- How AI outputs would integrate with existing APIs, payment gateways, subscription ledgers, CRM/support tools, notification systems, and account-access controls.
- Reliability requirements for billing-critical workflows, including latency, fallback behavior, model errors, duplicate charges, incorrect cancellations, and reconciliation with the source of truth.
- Privacy, security, compliance, and responsible AI concerns, especially around student data, payment data, eligibility status, explainability, and avoiding unfair treatment of vulnerable users.
- Product trade-offs between automation and human review, revenue recovery and customer trust, personalization and transparency, experimentation speed and operational risk.
- Rollout and observability needs, including phased launches, audit logs, monitoring for model drift, billing incident detection, escalation paths, and rollback plans.
- Success and guardrail signals such as recovered revenue, reduced involuntary churn, support contact rate, payment dispute rate, refund volume, user complaints, and billing accuracy.

Your goal is to frame a technically sound evaluation of AI in subscription billing: identify the highest-leverage use cases, clarify system and data requirements, surface major risks and mitigations, and explain how you would decide whether the AI layer is safe, useful, and trustworthy enough to launch for student subscribers.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling family account controls for cross-functional squads
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the Technical Product Manager for family account controls in a large-scale digital product used by parents, guardians, children, and teens across multiple devices and regions. The product lets families configure permissions such as content access, purchase approvals, screen-time limits, privacy settings, notifications, account recovery, and emergency overrides. The current experience is becoming slower and less reliable as usage grows and as multiple cross-functional squads add new control types, policy rules, surfaces, and compliance requirements.

Your task is to evaluate the technical trade-offs involved in scaling this family controls platform while making response time the primary product goal. Response time may include how quickly a guardian action takes effect, how quickly a child permission request is processed, how fast policy decisions are returned to client apps, and how quickly dependent systems can consume updated family-control state.

The scenario assumes multiple squads depend on the same family-control infrastructure, including identity, payments, content moderation, notifications, trust and safety, customer support, data platform, and regional compliance teams. You should frame the problem as a technical product decision: what must be designed, measured, prioritized, and governed so the platform can scale without degrading trust, safety, privacy, or developer velocity.

The experience should consider:
- Core user workflows, including setting controls, requesting exceptions, approving or denying requests, syncing settings across devices, and handling recovery or override cases.
- API and data-model requirements for representing family relationships, roles, permissions, policy rules, device state, and audit history.
- Response-time expectations for different paths, such as real-time enforcement, asynchronous propagation, notification delivery, and support/admin actions.
- Reliability trade-offs across caching, consistency, replication, event-driven updates, fallback behavior, and graceful degradation.
- Privacy, security, and compliance constraints involving minors’ data, parental consent, regional rules, access control, auditability, and data minimization.
- Cross-squad ownership boundaries, platform extensibility, versioning, dependency management, and safe rollout of new control types.
- Observability needs, including latency instrumentation, propagation delay tracking, policy-decision logs, error budgets, cohort analysis, and incident detection.
- Product trade-offs between fast response, correctness, scalability, operational complexity, user trust, and long-term platform maintainability.

Your goal is to structure a clear technical PM evaluation that identifies the key requirements, trade-offs, risks, and decision criteria for scaling family account controls, without jumping directly to a single architecture. The interviewer is looking for how you reason through system behavior, product impact, cross-functional constraints, and measurable response-time outcomes.

title: A competitor is attacking marketplace checkout and product discovery. What should Ecommerce do next?
description:
Problem Statement Description

Ecommerce operates a marketplace where buyers discover products through search, recommendations, category browsing, and seller listings, then complete purchases through checkout, payment, delivery, and returns flows. A competitor is gaining attention by improving both product discovery and checkout, creating pressure on Ecommerce’s purchase conversion, especially among first-time buyers who have lower trust and less familiarity with the marketplace.

You are being asked to define what Ecommerce should do next from a product strategy perspective. The response should frame the competitive threat, identify where Ecommerce may be vulnerable or advantaged, and evaluate strategic options across discovery, checkout, trust, seller quality, payments, and post-purchase confidence. The focus is not on designing a single feature, but on deciding where the company should place its bets and how it should sequence action.

Your strategy should consider customer, seller, marketplace, and business implications. It should also account for constraints such as catalog quality, seller incentives, payment reliability, privacy, accessibility, operational cost, and the risk of over-optimizing conversion at the expense of trust or long-term retention.

The experience should consider:
- Which user segment is most exposed to the competitor’s attack, especially first-time buyers and high-intent shoppers
- Where conversion is breaking down across discovery, product evaluation, cart, checkout, payment, and post-purchase confidence
- Strategic options such as improving relevance, trust signals, checkout speed, payment success, seller quality, pricing transparency, or returns confidence
- Ecommerce’s right to win based on marketplace scale, customer data, seller network, logistics, brand trust, or operational capabilities
- Trade-offs between short-term conversion gains and long-term marketplace health
- Risks around privacy, responsible personalization, seller gaming, accessibility, fraud, and operational load
- Decision gates and metrics that would indicate whether to invest, test, partner, copy, differentiate, or deprioritize

The goal is to present a clear strategic recommendation for how Ecommerce should respond to the competitor’s attack, including the reasoning behind the choice, the alternatives considered, the key risks, and how the company would know whether the strategy is working.

title: Tell me about a time you managed conflict across teams while pursuing retention in the context of team collaboration for power users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to describe a real situation where you managed conflict across teams while working on a retention-related initiative for power users of a team collaboration product. The setting should involve users who rely heavily on the product for daily workflows, coordination, knowledge sharing, project execution, or cross-functional communication.

Your story should show how you navigated disagreement between teams such as product, design, engineering, data, sales, customer success, support, legal, trust, or go-to-market. The conflict may have involved roadmap priorities, user needs, technical constraints, customer escalation, quality trade-offs, monetization pressure, or differing interpretations of retention data.

The interviewer is looking for evidence of how you created alignment without oversimplifying the tension. A strong response should make clear what was at stake for power users, why retention mattered, how the conflict affected execution or decision-making, and what role you personally played in moving the teams forward.

The experience should consider:
- The specific collaboration product context and the power-user workflow being affected
- The retention problem or risk, including how it was identified or measured
- The teams involved, their incentives, and the source of conflict
- Your personal ownership, decision-making role, and influence without authority
- How you used customer evidence, data, judgment, or principles to create alignment
- The trade-offs made across user value, business goals, technical feasibility, and team capacity
- The outcome, including impact on users, retention, team trust, or execution quality
- What you learned and how it changed your approach to cross-functional product leadership

The goal is to demonstrate your ability to lead through ambiguity and disagreement in a product environment where highly engaged users depend on the collaboration experience. Your answer should provide a concrete example with clear stakes, actions, impact, and reflection.

title: Tell me about a time you handled a difficult stakeholder while protecting successful application completion
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to share a real example of handling a difficult stakeholder in a government digital services environment, where citizens were trying to complete an application for benefits. The focus is on how you protected the user outcome—successful application completion—while navigating disagreement, pressure, delays, or conflicting priorities from a stakeholder.

Your story should be relevant to public-sector product work, where application flows may involve identity verification, eligibility checks, document uploads, multilingual support, accessibility requirements, fraud controls, legacy systems, policy teams, operations teams, and assisted service centers. The interviewer is looking for evidence that you can balance stakeholder management with service reliability, citizen trust, inclusion, privacy, and operational constraints.

Choose an example where the stakeholder conflict had real consequences for users or delivery, such as a policy owner pushing for extra form fields, a compliance team blocking a launch, an operations leader worried about support burden, an engineering team constrained by legacy systems, or a senior sponsor requesting a change that could reduce completion rates.

The experience should consider:
- What made the stakeholder difficult: conflicting goals, urgency, authority, communication style, risk tolerance, or misunderstanding of user impact
- The citizen application journey at risk, including where users could abandon, fail verification, submit incomplete data, or need assisted support
- Your specific role, ownership, and decision-making authority in the situation
- How you used evidence such as completion rates, support tickets, user research, accessibility findings, policy constraints, or operational data
- How you communicated trade-offs around inclusion, privacy, fraud prevention, cost, timelines, and service quality
- What actions you took to align the stakeholder without damaging trust or accountability
- The measurable or observable impact on application completion, launch readiness, user experience, or operational stability
- What you learned and how it changed your future approach to stakeholder management

The goal is to demonstrate a clear, credible story of product leadership: you protected a critical public-service outcome for citizens while constructively managing a challenging stakeholder in a high-accountability environment.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in team visibility for local services marketplace
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager for a local services marketplace where customers discover, compare, and contact service providers such as cleaners, plumbers, tutors, repair specialists, and home professionals. A key paid offering allows premium subscribers to showcase their teams or crews more prominently across search results, category pages, profile pages, and lead-matching experiences.

Over the past day, the business has observed a sudden drop in “team visibility” for premium subscribers. This could mean fewer premium teams appearing to customers, lower impressions in marketplace surfaces, reduced ranking presence, missing team cards, or degraded exposure in lead-generation flows. The issue is important because premium subscribers pay for enhanced visibility, and a sustained drop could affect trust, renewals, lead volume, and marketplace supply quality.

Your task is to diagnose the issue before recommending fixes. Focus on how you would frame the anomaly, validate that it is real, isolate affected users and surfaces, inspect instrumentation, generate hypotheses, gather evidence, and decide what immediate mitigations or longer-term prevention mechanisms may be needed.

The experience should consider:
- How “team visibility” is defined, including numerator, denominator, marketplace surface, and expected baseline.
- Which premium subscribers are affected by geography, service category, subscription tier, device, app/web surface, ranking bucket, or traffic source.
- Whether the drop is real user impact or a measurement, logging, dashboard, or data pipeline issue.
- Recent changes that could affect visibility, such as ranking updates, eligibility rules, subscription enforcement, moderation filters, inventory changes, experiments, or release rollouts.
- Marketplace-side factors such as demand shifts, customer search behavior, provider availability, team capacity, profile completeness, or location matching.
- How to compare premium subscribers against non-premium providers, historical cohorts, control groups, and unaffected regions or categories.
- What evidence would be needed before escalating, rolling back, communicating with affected subscribers, or applying temporary mitigation.
- How to prevent recurrence through monitoring, alerting, ownership, QA checks, and clearer visibility health metrics.

The goal is to demonstrate a structured root-cause analysis approach for a hard marketplace incident: clarify the metric, determine blast radius, separate instrumentation from product reality, prioritize hypotheses, identify the most likely cause using evidence, and outline how the team should stabilize the experience without prematurely jumping to a fix.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in meeting follow-through for developer API portal
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager for a developer API portal used by family accounts to set up, manage, or troubleshoot API-enabled services. A key downstream behavior, “meeting follow-through,” has suddenly dropped for the family segment. This could include users not attending scheduled onboarding/support meetings, not completing required pre-meeting steps, or not taking the expected action after a meeting.

Your task is to diagnose the drop before proposing fixes. Treat this as a hard root-cause analysis: clarify what changed, validate whether the anomaly is real, identify where in the workflow the decline occurs, and separate product, operational, data, and external causes.

Assume the workflow may involve portal login, API app/project selection, eligibility checks, meeting scheduling, calendar/email reminders, pre-meeting documentation, attendance, and post-meeting completion. Families may have additional constraints around multiple household members, permissions, time zones, accessibility, privacy, and trust.

The experience should consider:
- The exact definition of “meeting follow-through,” including numerator, denominator, time window, and whether it measures attendance, completion, or post-meeting action.
- Segmentation by family account type, geography, device, browser, language, API product, meeting type, lifecycle stage, and acquisition channel.
- Instrumentation checks for event logging, calendar integrations, reminder delivery, attendance tracking, attribution, and recent schema or dashboard changes.
- Funnel analysis across scheduling, confirmation, reminder receipt, pre-work completion, meeting join, and post-meeting task completion.
- Recent changes in the portal, authentication, permissions, notification systems, API documentation, support operations, or meeting vendor integrations.
- Hypotheses that distinguish user behavior changes from system failures, operational capacity issues, policy changes, seasonality, or external calendar/email deliverability problems.
- Evidence needed to prioritize causes, including logs, cohort comparisons, support tickets, failed API calls, user session traces, and qualitative feedback.
- Short-term containment, long-term prevention, and monitoring needed once the cause is confirmed.

The goal is to structure a rigorous RCA that would help the team confidently identify the source of the sudden drop, understand its user and business impact, and determine what evidence is required before moving into fixes.

title: Create a launch plan for B2B onboarding console aimed at clinic administrators
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are responsible for launching a new B2B onboarding console for clinic administrators. The console is intended to help administrators set up their clinic, invite staff, configure workflows, connect required systems, understand compliance-related steps, and reach a state where the product is meaningfully usable by the clinic rather than merely “activated.”

This is an execution-focused question. Your task is not to redesign the console itself, but to create a practical launch plan that can move the product from readiness to adoption across clinic customers. The launch should optimize for useful engagement: administrators completing setup actions that lead to real operational value, not just logging in once or clicking through screens.

Assume clinic administrators are busy, risk-sensitive users who may be coordinating with clinicians, IT contacts, billing teams, and customer support. The launch plan should account for customer readiness, onboarding complexity, operational support, internal dependencies, and signals that indicate whether the rollout is working.

The launch plan should consider:
- Target clinic segments for initial rollout, such as small practices, multi-location clinics, or enterprise healthcare groups
- Key onboarding milestones and what “useful engagement” means in measurable behavioral terms
- Owners and dependencies across product, engineering, sales, customer success, support, compliance, and implementation teams
- Sequencing of launch phases, including pilot, limited availability, broader rollout, and post-launch iteration
- Go/no-go criteria, readiness checks, training needs, and support coverage before expanding access
- Instrumentation needed to monitor setup completion, feature usage, drop-off points, support burden, and customer outcomes
- Risks such as workflow disruption, incorrect configuration, low admin adoption, compliance concerns, or overloading support teams
- Rollback, escalation, and communication plans for both internal teams and clinic customers

The goal is to present a launch plan that shows strong execution judgment: how you would coordinate teams, reduce launch risk, measure meaningful adoption, and ensure clinic administrators successfully move from initial access to productive use of the onboarding console.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling identity verification flow for customer success teams
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale an identity verification flow used by customer success teams in a large-scale digital product. Agents rely on this flow to confirm a customer’s identity before taking sensitive actions such as account recovery, transaction support, profile updates, or escalation handling. The product goal is search success: agents must be able to find the right customer record, verification context, and next-best action quickly and accurately, without increasing fraud, privacy risk, or operational burden.

The current experience may involve multiple systems, inconsistent identifiers, manual review steps, regional compliance differences, and varying data quality across customer profiles. As volume grows across markets and support channels, the technical PM must reason about how identity signals, search infrastructure, verification APIs, risk systems, and agent tooling should work together while preserving latency, auditability, and trust.

This is a technical product trade-off discussion. You are not expected to design a full architecture in code, but you should be able to define requirements, identify system constraints, compare implementation options, and explain how technical decisions affect agent productivity, customer safety, regulatory exposure, and search outcomes.

The experience should consider:
- The end-to-end workflow for a customer success agent: searching for a user, selecting the correct account, triggering or reviewing verification, and resolving the case.
- Data and API requirements, including identity attributes, account identifiers, verification status, risk signals, consent, audit logs, and integration points with CRM/support tools.
- Search success definition, including result relevance, match accuracy, false positives, false negatives, latency, fallback paths, and agent confidence.
- Reliability and scale needs across high-volume support periods, global regions, multiple languages, incomplete records, duplicate accounts, and degraded downstream services.
- Privacy, security, and compliance constraints around personally identifiable information, access controls, data minimization, retention, encryption, and regulatory differences.
- Trade-offs between automation and human review, speed and risk, centralized and federated data models, strict matching and fuzzy matching, and build-versus-integrate decisions.
- Rollout and observability requirements, including experimentation, phased launches, monitoring, incident response, abuse detection, and quality feedback loops from agents.
- Product risks such as customer lockout, account takeover, biased verification outcomes, poor accessibility, agent workarounds, and loss of trust.

Your goal is to evaluate the technical trade-offs and scope a scalable identity verification experience that improves search success for customer success teams while maintaining safety, compliance, reliability, and a usable agent workflow.

title: Describe a product failure or missed launch that taught you a lesson relevant to food-delivery under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to share a real example of a product failure, missed launch, or materially underperforming rollout from your own experience, and connect the lessons to a Swiggy-like food-delivery environment. The context to keep in mind is group ordering for office lunches, where an office coordinator may collect preferences, manage budgets or reimbursements, coordinate delivery timing, and place repeat orders for teams.

This is a behavioral question, so the focus is not on designing a new feature. The interviewer is looking for evidence of how you personally handled ambiguity, ownership, stakeholder pressure, operational complexity, and post-failure learning. Your story should show how you diagnosed what went wrong, what trade-offs you made, how you communicated, and how the experience would shape your judgment in a marketplace business operating at high scale.

In this domain, failures can come from many sources: restaurant prep-time variability, delivery partner batching, incorrect incentives, unreliable demand forecasts, privacy or consent issues in group ordering, accessibility gaps, poor data quality, or regulatory constraints around payments, discounts, food safety, and customer communication. Your example should make clear why the failure mattered to users, the business, and operations.

The experience should consider:
- The specific product, launch, or initiative you owned, and your role in the outcome.
- The user workflow affected, especially any coordinator, group, merchant, or operations-facing friction.
- The assumptions you or the team made about incentives, scale, compliance, user behavior, or operational readiness.
- What signals showed the launch was failing or at risk, such as adoption, repeat usage, cancellations, complaints, SLA misses, or partner escalations.
- How you responded in the moment, including stakeholder communication, mitigation, trade-off decisions, or launch rollback.
- What you learned about building products where marketplace liquidity, delivery reliability, incentives, and trust are tightly connected.
- How that lesson would apply to improving repeat office group orders in a Swiggy-like environment without overloading restaurants, delivery partners, or support teams.

Your goal is to tell a concise but substantive story that demonstrates senior product judgment: ownership of the miss, clear reasoning under constraints, measurable impact, humility, and a transferable lesson for building reliable food-delivery products at scale.

title: Define success metrics for AI writing review serving freelancers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating an AI writing review product built for freelancers who submit client-facing work such as articles, proposals, marketing copy, reports, or profile content and receive automated feedback before delivery. The product aims to help freelancers review more writing with less manual effort while maintaining quality, trust, and usability.

The business priority is operational throughput: how much useful review work the system can complete efficiently across many freelancers, writing formats, languages, and quality levels. Your task is to define a metrics framework that can show whether the AI review experience is increasing productive review capacity without creating hidden quality, latency, cost, or trust problems.

Focus on how success should be measured across the full workflow: submission, AI analysis, feedback generation, freelancer review, revision, and eventual use of the output. Assume the product team needs metrics that are actionable for product, operations, model quality, and business stakeholders.

The experience should consider:
- A clear definition of the primary throughput metric, including numerator, denominator, and time window.
- How to distinguish completed, useful reviews from low-quality, abandoned, duplicate, or reworked reviews.
- Instrumentation needed across upload, processing, feedback delivery, revision, acceptance, and export/share steps.
- Relevant freelancer cohorts, such as new versus repeat users, high-volume freelancers, writing category, language, geography, or device type.
- Quality and trust guardrails, including feedback usefulness, accuracy concerns, user overrides, complaints, and client-impact signals.
- Operational constraints such as AI processing latency, review queue capacity, cost per review, failure rates, and human escalation needs.
- Decision usefulness: how the metrics would help diagnose whether throughput gains come from adoption, frequency, automation efficiency, or reduced friction.

Your goal is to propose a practical success-measurement approach that helps the team decide whether AI writing review is scaling freelancer productivity responsibly, efficiently, and reliably.

title: Create a launch plan for a high-risk Gmail feature for creators

- Scope: phased launch over 6-8 weeks

Key terms
- allowlists: A list of users or entities permitted to access a feature
- go/no-go decision gates: Criteria used to decide whether to proceed with a launch

How you'll be evaluated
Prioritization · Planning and sequencing · Stakeholder alignment · Launch criteria

title: Design a privacy-safe personalization system for Business Travel
description:
About Airbnb

Context
Airbnb is enhancing Business Travel experiences with personalized recommendations while ensuring user privacy. This involves balancing personalization with data trust and compliance across various user expectations.

Key details

- Situation: improving Business Travel experience
- Goal: personalize recommendations and booking flows

Key terms
- Superhost: High-quality hosts recognized for exceptional hospitality

How you'll be evaluated
System understanding · Technical trade-offs · Scalability and reliability · Communication

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for offline order capture among freelancers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are estimating the annual opportunity for a product that helps freelancers capture offline orders more reliably and connect those orders to dependable payment collection. These freelancers may receive work requests through calls, messages, in-person conversations, referrals, or social platforms, but often lack a structured way to record the order, confirm scope, track delivery, and ensure they get paid on time.

The estimate should focus on the size of the yearly opportunity: how many freelancers could use such a workflow, how often they receive offline orders, the typical value of those orders, and what portion of order value is affected by payment delays, disputes, partial payments, or non-payment. The answer should make clear whether you are estimating total transaction value, addressable product opportunity, revenue opportunity, or value unlocked through improved payment reliability.

This is a guesstimate problem, so the emphasis is on structuring the market logically, stating assumptions, sizing key drivers, and testing whether the result is directionally reasonable. You may choose a geography, freelancer definition, and monetization lens, but you should make those choices explicit and keep the calculation internally consistent.

The experience should consider:
- The target freelancer segments included, such as designers, tutors, consultants, photographers, local service providers, creators, or gig professionals.
- The scope of “offline order capture,” including orders initiated through phone, chat, walk-ins, referrals, paper notes, or informal conversations.
- The unit of estimation: freelancers, orders per year, gross order value, payment failure value, or potential product revenue.
- Adoption assumptions, including which freelancers have enough order volume or payment pain to use a dedicated tool.
- Frequency and average order value assumptions by freelancer type or income tier.
- Payment reliability factors, such as delayed payments, cancellations, disputes, lack of upfront deposits, and missing order records.
- Sensitivity of the estimate to the largest assumptions, especially freelancer population, order frequency, and payment failure rate.
- Sanity checks against income levels, total freelance market size, and realistic willingness to pay or transaction take-rate.

The goal is to produce a clear, defensible annual opportunity estimate and explain how offline order capture could translate into more reliable payments for freelancers, without jumping directly to a product solution.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling partner integration marketplace for growth marketers
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the Technical PM for a partner integration marketplace used by growth marketers to discover, configure, and manage integrations with tools such as ad platforms, CRMs, analytics providers, email systems, attribution tools, and data warehouses. As the marketplace scales to more partners, more customers, and more integration types, support teams are seeing repetitive tickets around setup failures, unclear permissions, sync errors, webhook delays, missing data, version mismatches, and partner-specific troubleshooting.

Your task is to evaluate the technical trade-offs involved in scaling this marketplace with support deflection as the primary product goal. The focus is not only on adding more integrations, but on making the integration experience more self-serve, diagnosable, reliable, and understandable for non-technical growth marketers while still meeting platform, partner, security, and operational constraints.

Consider the full workflow: a marketer searches for an integration, evaluates compatibility, connects accounts, grants permissions, maps fields or events, monitors sync health, receives error guidance, and resolves issues without needing to contact support. You should frame the technical decisions that would shape this experience, the risks they introduce, and how you would evaluate whether they improve support deflection.

The experience should consider:
- Integration architecture trade-offs, such as standardized connector frameworks versus custom partner-specific implementations.
- API and data requirements, including authentication, permissions, rate limits, schema mapping, webhook handling, retries, and error normalization.
- Reliability expectations for data sync, partner availability, latency, failure recovery, and graceful degradation.
- Self-serve troubleshooting needs, including actionable error messages, integration health status, logs, setup validation, and guided resolution paths.
- Privacy and security constraints around customer credentials, OAuth scopes, data sharing, auditability, and partner access.
- Observability and instrumentation needed to identify failure patterns, ticket drivers, partner quality issues, and deflection opportunities.
- Rollout considerations for new integrations, partner certification, versioning, backward compatibility, and migration from legacy flows.
- Product trade-offs between marketplace breadth, integration depth, ease of use, operational cost, partner autonomy, and customer trust.

The goal is to assess how you reason through technical product decisions in a scaled integration ecosystem. Your response should define the problem space, identify the key architectural and product trade-offs, explain what data or signals you would use to make decisions, and show how the resulting marketplace experience could reduce avoidable support interactions while maintaining reliability, security, and marketer confidence.

title: Decide whether to invest in family account controls for first-time buyers to improve task completion
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether a large-scale consumer or marketplace product should invest in family account controls to help first-time buyers complete their intended tasks. First-time buyers may be unfamiliar with account setup, payment decisions, permissions, trust signals, purchase confirmation, or post-purchase coordination, and some may rely on a parent, spouse, caregiver, or household member to review or approve actions.

The proposed investment could include shared family profiles, role-based permissions, spending limits, approval flows, delegated task completion, notifications, or visibility into orders and account activity. The strategic question is whether these controls would materially improve first-time buyer task completion enough to justify the product, engineering, design, policy, support, and trust-and-safety investment.

You should treat this as a product strategy decision, not a feature design exercise. Consider the target users, market need, business impact, alternatives, risks, and how the company would decide whether to build, test, scale, or defer this investment.

The experience should consider:
- Which first-time buyer segments are most likely to need family account controls, and why task completion breaks down today.
- The size and importance of the opportunity relative to other ways to improve first-time buyer completion.
- Strategic options, including building full family controls, testing lightweight approval/sharing features, improving onboarding, or investing elsewhere.
- The company’s right to win, including trust, identity, payments, privacy, safety, and cross-device capabilities.
- Trade-offs around added friction, consent, family dynamics, fraud risk, regulatory exposure, accessibility, and support complexity.
- How success would be measured, including completion lift, activation, repeat usage, trust, conversion quality, and unintended consequences.
- Decision gates for experimentation, rollout, operational readiness, and when to stop or expand the investment.

Your goal is to make a clear recommendation on whether to invest, explaining the strategic rationale, key assumptions, expected impact, major risks, and what evidence would be needed to move forward confidently.

title: Define success metrics for remote training platform serving fleet coordinators
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a remote training platform used by fleet coordinators, whose day-to-day work includes coordinating drivers, dispatch updates, maintenance issues, compliance tasks, and recurring operational meetings. The business wants to understand whether the platform is actually improving meeting follow-through, not just whether users are consuming training content.

In this context, “meeting follow-through” may involve coordinators attending required sessions, completing agreed action items, updating stakeholders, and applying what they learned in live fleet operations. The challenge is to define metrics that connect training engagement to real operational behavior while accounting for coordinator workload, shift schedules, regional differences, and data quality limitations.

Your task is to propose a practical success-measurement framework for the platform. Focus on what should be measured, how the metrics should be defined, what denominators and cohorts matter, how instrumentation would work, and how the metrics would help product and business teams make decisions.

The measurement framework should consider:
- A clear definition of the primary success outcome for meeting follow-through and the denominator used to calculate it.
- Leading indicators across the training journey, such as enrollment, attendance, completion, comprehension, and engagement quality.
- Downstream behavior after training, including whether coordinators act on meeting commitments in a timely and reliable way.
- Instrumentation across the training platform, calendar or meeting tools, task systems, and operational workflows.
- Cohorts such as new versus experienced coordinators, fleet size, region, shift pattern, training module, and manager/team structure.
- Guardrail metrics to ensure the platform does not increase coordinator burden, reduce operational responsiveness, or incentivize low-quality task completion.
- Data reliability concerns, including missing integrations, manual updates, duplicate meetings, and inconsistent action-item tracking.
- Decision usefulness, including how the metrics would inform product iteration, training content changes, rollout decisions, and customer success interventions.

The goal is to define a metrics system that fairly evaluates whether remote training improves real meeting follow-through for fleet coordinators and provides actionable insight for improving the product and operational outcomes.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in repeat usage for loyalty rewards engine
description:
Problem Statement Description

A loyalty rewards engine is used by billing admins to manage and revisit reward-related workflows such as configuring reward rules, reviewing earned rewards, applying credits or discounts, reconciling billing adjustments, and monitoring program spend. Recently, repeat usage by billing admins has dropped suddenly, meaning fewer admins are coming back to use the engine after prior usage.

Your task is to diagnose what may have caused the drop before proposing any fixes. Treat this as a real product incident where the decline could be caused by product changes, billing workflow disruption, seasonality, permissions, data quality, customer mix, reporting issues, or measurement errors. The focus is not to jump to solutions, but to structure the investigation and identify the most likely root cause with evidence.

Assume this product has multiple admin roles, account tiers, reward program types, integrations with billing systems, and operational dependencies such as invoices, credits, approval flows, and audit logs. Billing admins are time-sensitive users who rely on accuracy, trust, and predictable workflows, so any issue affecting visibility, correctness, or completion confidence could influence whether they return.

The diagnosis should consider:
- How to define the repeat usage drop, including time window, baseline, denominator, and whether the metric reflects active admins, accounts, sessions, or completed reward workflows
- Whether the anomaly is real or caused by instrumentation, event tracking, identity mapping, role changes, bot filtering, logging delays, or dashboard changes
- Segmentation by account size, region, billing cycle, admin role, reward program type, integration type, platform, and new versus existing customers
- Funnel and workflow analysis across key admin actions such as login, program selection, reward review, approval, credit application, export, and reconciliation
- Product, policy, pricing, permission, API, or billing-system changes that coincided with the drop
- External or cyclical factors such as billing periods, fiscal close, promotional campaigns ending, customer churn, or support escalations
- Qualitative evidence from support tickets, customer success notes, admin feedback, audit logs, and failed task patterns
- Immediate containment needs, longer-term prevention, and how to communicate findings without overclaiming before evidence is validated

The goal is to present a clear root-cause investigation plan that narrows the problem from a broad usage decline into testable hypotheses, validates or eliminates likely causes, and identifies what evidence would be needed before recommending product, operational, or measurement fixes.

title: Retention fell after a redesign of privacy controls. Investigate the issue
description:
Problem Statement Description

A large-scale technology product recently redesigned its privacy controls experience for administrators. The redesign was intended to make privacy settings easier to understand, improve trust, and give admins better control over how user or organizational data is managed. Soon after launch, retention declined among administrator accounts.

Your task is to investigate the retention drop as a root-cause analysis. Focus on understanding whether the decline is truly caused by the privacy controls redesign, which administrator segments are affected, and what evidence would help separate product friction, trust concerns, instrumentation issues, seasonality, or external factors.

Assume the privacy controls are used by admins who configure data-sharing, visibility, consent, access, or compliance-related settings for their teams or organizations. Changes in this area may affect confidence, perceived safety, setup effort, and downstream usage by end users, so the investigation should account for both behavioral metrics and trust-related signals.

The experience should consider:
- How to define the retention metric, including the retention window, denominator, and what counts as an active retained administrator
- Whether the drop is visible across all admins or concentrated by segment, such as new vs. existing admins, organization size, geography, plan type, role permissions, or compliance-sensitive customers
- Whether the redesign changed key workflows, such as finding settings, understanding defaults, saving changes, inviting users, approving permissions, or completing compliance tasks
- Instrumentation checks to confirm that the retention decline is not caused by tracking changes, event renames, missing logs, consent changes, or dashboard errors
- Hypotheses related to usability friction, unexpected defaults, loss of trust, increased setup time, broken permissions, unclear language, or policy-compliance concerns
- Evidence sources such as funnel data, cohort retention, support tickets, admin feedback, session replays, audit logs, error rates, and qualitative research
- Short-term mitigation options and longer-term prevention mechanisms without assuming the redesign must be fully rolled back

The goal is to structure a clear, evidence-driven investigation that identifies the most likely cause of the retention decline, proposes how to validate it, and outlines how the product team should respond while protecting customer trust and administrator confidence.

title: Tell me about a time you managed conflict across teams while pursuing operational efficiency in the context of data export tool for finance teams
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to share a real example of managing cross-team conflict while improving operational efficiency for finance teams using a data export tool. The situation should involve a product or workflow where finance users depend on timely, accurate, and configurable exports for activities such as reconciliation, reporting, audits, month-end close, forecasting, compliance, or downstream analysis.

Focus on a conflict that required you to align teams with different priorities, such as engineering, data platform, finance operations, compliance, security, customer support, or go-to-market teams. The conflict may have involved scope, timelines, data quality, system performance, access controls, export formats, ownership of defects, manual workarounds, or trade-offs between speed and accuracy.

Your story should show how you understood the operational pain, clarified the business impact, handled disagreement constructively, and drove progress without simply escalating or compromising on critical user needs. The interviewer is looking for evidence of ownership, judgment, stakeholder management, communication, and measurable impact in a product environment serving finance users.

The experience should consider:
- The finance-team workflow being improved and why the export process mattered operationally
- The specific teams involved and what each side was optimizing for
- The nature of the conflict, including constraints around data accuracy, security, reliability, or delivery timelines
- How you diagnosed the root cause of disagreement and separated user needs from team preferences
- The actions you took to align stakeholders, make trade-offs, and maintain momentum
- The operational efficiency outcome, such as reduced manual effort, faster close cycles, fewer support tickets, or improved export reliability
- How you communicated decisions, risks, and progress across technical and business stakeholders
- What you learned about managing conflict in data-heavy or finance-sensitive product areas

Your goal is to present a concise but complete behavioral story that demonstrates how you led through ambiguity and disagreement, protected trust in financial data workflows, and delivered a meaningful efficiency improvement for users and the business.

title: Evaluate technical trade-offs for scaling document collaboration flow for fleet coordinators
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating how to scale a document collaboration flow used by fleet coordinators who manage operational documents across vehicles, drivers, dispatch teams, vendors, and compliance stakeholders. These users may collaborate on items such as driver credentials, vehicle inspection records, maintenance approvals, delivery paperwork, insurance documents, and incident reports, often under time-sensitive operating conditions.

The product goal is conversion: turning more qualified fleet teams from initial interest, trial, or limited usage into successful active customers. The collaboration experience must therefore feel reliable, fast, secure, and easy enough for coordinators to invite others, complete key document workflows, and trust the platform for daily operations.

As a Technical PM, your task is to evaluate the technical trade-offs involved in scaling this flow. Consider what must change as usage grows across larger fleets, more document types, more collaborators, higher concurrency, stricter permissions, and potentially distributed teams operating across locations and time zones. Do not assume unlimited engineering capacity; focus on the trade-offs that matter most for conversion and long-term product quality.

The experience should consider:
- Core user workflows, including document upload, sharing, commenting, approval, versioning, notifications, and completion tracking.
- Data and API requirements for document metadata, permissions, audit trails, collaborator roles, workflow state, and integrations with fleet-management or compliance systems.
- Reliability and performance expectations for large files, high-volume fleets, real-time or near-real-time collaboration, offline/poor-connectivity scenarios, and peak operational periods.
- Privacy, security, and compliance needs, including role-based access, sensitive driver or vehicle data, encryption, retention, auditability, and external collaborator access.
- Technical architecture trade-offs such as synchronous vs. asynchronous processing, real-time collaboration vs. simpler state updates, centralized vs. distributed document storage, and build vs. integrate decisions.
- Observability and instrumentation needed to understand collaboration bottlenecks, failed uploads, invite completion, permission errors, latency, workflow drop-offs, and conversion impact.
- Rollout strategy, including migration risks, backwards compatibility, feature flags, staged launches, support readiness, and rollback plans.
- Product trade-offs between speed to market, user simplicity, scalability, cost, operational complexity, and trust.

Your goal is to frame a technically sound product evaluation that connects engineering choices to user adoption and conversion. The interviewer is looking for how you define requirements, reason through trade-offs, identify risks, and decide what technical investments are necessary to make the collaboration flow scalable and commercially effective for fleet coordinators.

title: You're the PM for our stock trading product. With gross profit dropping significantly over the last month, what would you do?

Goal clarity · Metric selection · Trade-offs and guardrails · Measurement plan

title: How would you design parking features on Google Maps?

Users need effective parking solutions while using Google Maps. Different user needs must be understood for feature design.
