System understanding · Technical trade-offs · Scalability and reliability · Communication

title: How would you measure success for a Real Estate-style rental home search and verification launch under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints?
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the PM for a real estate marketplace launching a rental home search and listing verification experience for relocating renters. These users are making high-stakes decisions from a distance, often under time pressure, and need confidence that listings are available, accurate, legal, and worth contacting before they invest time in tours, applications, or broker conversations.

The launch is expected to improve the quality of property leads sent to landlords, brokers, or property managers while maintaining renter trust at scale. However, the system operates with constraints: listing data can become stale quickly, brokers may have incentives to keep low-quality or unavailable listings live, offline verification can be expensive, and rental rules vary across local markets.

In this metrics interview, define how you would measure whether the launch is successful. Focus on building a measurement framework that distinguishes renter value, marketplace trust, lead quality, operational efficiency, and compliance risk rather than relying only on surface-level engagement.

The experience should consider:
- The primary success metric and its precise definition, including numerator, denominator, time window, and what qualifies as a “verified” listing or “qualified” property lead
- Funnel instrumentation from search impression to listing view, verification signal exposure, contact/lead submission, broker response, tour/application intent, and downstream outcome
- Cohorts such as relocating renters vs local renters, new vs returning users, high-demand vs low-supply markets, verified vs unverified inventory, and broker-managed vs owner-managed listings
- Data freshness and accuracy signals, including availability, price, photos, location, amenities, fees, policy details, and last verification timestamp
- Guardrail metrics for trust, fairness, privacy, accessibility, regulatory compliance, lead spam, broker manipulation, and renter complaints
- Operational metrics such as verification cost per active listing, manual review load, SLA adherence, false positives/false negatives, and scalability across cities
- Decision usefulness: how the metrics would inform whether to expand, pause, change verification depth, adjust ranking, or invest further in operations and automation

Your goal is to present a clear success measurement approach that helps leadership judge whether the launch creates a more trustworthy and efficient rental marketplace for relocating renters while producing high-quality leads without unsustainable cost, compliance exposure, or ecosystem abuse.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for AI meeting assistant among new users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are estimating the annual opportunity for an AI meeting assistant targeted at new users. The product helps people capture, summarize, search, and act on meeting content, but new users may struggle with setup, permissions, calendar integrations, recording consent, transcript quality, summary expectations, and understanding how to use AI-generated outputs.

Frame the opportunity as both a user adoption problem and an operational leverage problem. The estimate should quantify the annual addressable opportunity among new users and connect it to support deflection: reducing avoidable help-center visits, support tickets, live chat contacts, onboarding questions, and setup-related escalations.

Your task is not to design the assistant or propose features. It is to build a structured guesstimate that defines the population, adoption funnel, usage frequency, likely support-contact behavior, and the portion of support volume that could reasonably be deflected through better AI assistance, onboarding, or in-product guidance.

The experience should consider:

- The scope of “new users”: newly registered users, newly activated workspace members, trial users, first-time meeting assistant users, or first-year customers.
- The unit of opportunity: annual users, meetings assisted, support contacts avoided, support cost saved, incremental retained users, or revenue impact.
- Population sizing assumptions across individuals, teams, or organizations using meeting-heavy workflows.
- Adoption and activation assumptions, including calendar connection, bot permissioning, first meeting captured, and repeat usage.
- Frequency assumptions such as meetings per user, meetings eligible for assistance, and support issues per new user.
- Support-deflection linkage, including which issues are deflectable versus those requiring human intervention.
- Sensitivity drivers, such as enterprise versus SMB mix, AI accuracy, privacy concerns, consent requirements, and onboarding complexity.
- Sanity checks against plausible meeting volume, support-contact rates, and cost-to-serve ranges.

The goal is to produce a clear, defensible annual estimate with transparent assumptions, logical segmentation, and a credible bridge from new-user adoption to support deflection impact.

title: Estimate revenue potential for payments checkout if adoption improves checkout success
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are asked to estimate the revenue potential of a payments checkout product serving local merchants, assuming merchant adoption of the checkout experience increases and that improved adoption leads to higher checkout success. The focus is on building a clear, defensible guesstimate rather than finding a precise market number.

Frame the problem from the perspective of a payments provider evaluating whether improved checkout adoption among local merchants could create meaningful incremental revenue. Local merchants may include small retailers, restaurants, service providers, and neighborhood businesses that accept digital payments online, in-app, or through payment links.

Your estimate should connect the merchant base, transaction volume, checkout success rate, payment take rate, and incremental revenue impact. You should make assumptions explicit, separate merchant adoption from shopper checkout completion, and avoid double-counting existing successful transactions.

The experience should consider:
- The geographic and merchant scope you are estimating for, such as a city, country, or broader market
- The unit of estimation, such as annual revenue, monthly revenue, or incremental payment volume
- The number of local merchants likely to use digital checkout and the share that could adopt the improved solution
- Average transaction frequency, average order value, and payment volume per merchant
- Current versus improved checkout success rates and how much incremental completed payment volume this creates
- The payments provider’s monetization model, such as take rate, fixed transaction fee, or software/payment bundle revenue
- Key assumptions and sensitivity drivers, especially adoption rate, merchant activity level, order value, and success-rate uplift
- Sanity checks to ensure the estimate is realistic relative to merchant behavior, payment volumes, and market size

Your goal is to produce a structured, transparent estimate of incremental revenue potential and explain which assumptions matter most to the business case.

title: Plan an MVP rollout for marketplace trust without disrupting existing users
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager responsible for rolling out an MVP trust layer for a marketplace used by enterprise teams to evaluate, select, and transact with vendors, service providers, apps, or partners. Enterprise buyers are cautious because trust gaps—unclear provider quality, insufficient verification, weak reviews, compliance uncertainty, or poor dispute visibility—can slow evaluation and reduce conversion.

Your task is to plan the MVP rollout in a way that improves buyer confidence and conversion without disrupting existing marketplace users, sellers, or ongoing transactions. The rollout should account for an active marketplace with existing search, discovery, listing, checkout/contact, and account workflows where sudden trust changes could affect seller visibility, buyer behavior, support load, or revenue.

Focus on execution: how you would sequence the rollout, coordinate teams, manage dependencies, define launch readiness, monitor risk, and decide whether to expand, pause, or roll back. You do not need to design the full trust system, but you should make clear what the MVP includes at a rollout level and how you would introduce it safely.

The experience should consider:
- The primary users affected, including enterprise buyers, marketplace sellers/providers, internal operations, support, sales, and risk/compliance teams
- The current buyer workflow and where trust signals would be introduced without creating confusion or friction
- MVP scope, non-goals, and what must be operationally ready before launch
- Rollout sequencing, such as internal testing, limited cohorts, marketplace category pilots, geography/account segmentation, or staged exposure
- Owners, dependencies, and coordination across product, engineering, data, design, legal, operations, support, and go-to-market teams
- Go/no-go criteria, launch metrics, guardrails, and decision checkpoints tied to conversion, engagement, seller impact, support burden, and marketplace health
- Risk mitigation, rollback plans, customer communication, seller enablement, and handling of edge cases or disputes
- Post-launch monitoring and iteration plan to expand the MVP responsibly

The goal is to present a practical operating plan that demonstrates how you would launch a trust-focused marketplace MVP with minimal disruption, measurable impact on enterprise conversion, and clear mechanisms to detect issues, protect marketplace participants, and scale only when the rollout is working.

title: Set launch metrics for an experiment in appointment booking with high trust risk
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating an experiment in an appointment-booking product used by remote teams to coordinate meetings across calendars, time zones, roles, and availability constraints. The experiment is intended to improve successful bookings, but it carries high trust risk because mistakes can lead to missed meetings, double bookings, incorrect attendees, privacy concerns, or users losing confidence in the scheduling flow.

Candidates should define the launch metrics that would determine whether the experiment is safe and valuable to ship. The focus is not only on whether more bookings happen, but whether those bookings are reliable, intentional, and trusted by both organizers and invitees.

The metrics plan should cover how success is measured, what the correct denominator is, how the experiment is instrumented, which user cohorts need separate analysis, and what guardrails would prevent a misleading launch decision.

The experience should consider:
- The end-to-end booking funnel from intent, availability selection, invite sending, confirmation, changes, cancellations, and meeting completion.
- Clear definitions of “successful booking,” including whether it means confirmed, attended, not cancelled, or completed without user complaint.
- Appropriate denominators, such as booking attempts, eligible users, organizers, invitees, teams, or calendar-connected accounts.
- Instrumentation needed to distinguish user actions, system-generated actions, calendar sync events, failures, edits, and reversals.
- Cohorts such as remote teams across time zones, new versus existing users, team size, organizer versus invitee, calendar provider, and device/platform.
- Trust and quality guardrails, including errors, duplicate bookings, incorrect time zones, privacy-related incidents, unexpected calendar changes, support contacts, and negative feedback.
- Decision usefulness: how the metrics would support launch, rollback, iteration, or further experimentation under uncertainty.

The goal is to produce a practical launch-metrics framework that helps a product team decide whether the experiment improves appointment booking outcomes while preserving user trust in a high-stakes scheduling workflow.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for customer feedback hub among security teams
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the annual opportunity for a customer feedback hub designed for security teams. The product would centralize signals such as customer-reported security concerns, compliance feedback, vulnerability-related requests, trust-center questions, support escalations, and product feedback from enterprise buyers or internal customer-facing teams.

The estimate should quantify the size of the opportunity in a way that is useful for product prioritization, not just market sizing. You should define what “opportunity” means: revenue potential, cost savings, support deflection, increased conversion, retention impact, or some combination tied to better self-serve success.

A key part of the problem is connecting the feedback hub to self-serve outcomes. For example, security teams may use customer feedback to improve documentation, automate answers, prioritize trust artifacts, reduce manual review cycles, or help customers resolve security concerns without needing direct human support.

The experience should consider:
- The target population of security teams, including company size, maturity, industry, and whether they sell B2B, SaaS, fintech, AI, or enterprise software products.
- The unit of analysis, such as number of companies, number of security teams, number of security practitioners, or number of customer-facing security workflows.
- Adoption assumptions for a customer feedback hub, including willingness to pay, build-versus-buy behavior, and existing tooling overlap.
- Frequency and volume of relevant customer feedback, such as security questionnaires, trust requests, vulnerability reports, compliance questions, and support escalations.
- How self-serve success could be measured, including deflected tickets, faster customer answers, reduced sales/security review time, improved trust-center usage, or higher conversion.
- Revenue and/or savings model assumptions, including pricing approach, annual contract value, seat-based pricing, usage-based pricing, or operational cost reduction.
- Sensitivity drivers, such as enterprise penetration, average feedback volume, automation rate, gross margin, and the share of workflows that can realistically become self-serve.
- Sanity checks against adjacent markets, existing security tooling budgets, support costs, and the typical workload of security, sales engineering, and customer success teams.

Your goal is to produce a structured, defensible annual opportunity estimate and explain how the estimate informs whether investing in this customer feedback hub can meaningfully improve self-serve success for security teams and their customers.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for first-time buyer onboarding among project managers
description:
Problem Statement Description

Estimate the annual opportunity for improving onboarding for project managers who are buying a product or service for the first time. In this context, “first-time buyer” means a project manager who has newly purchased, subscribed to, or initiated a paid team/workspace account and is going through the early setup journey before the product becomes part of their regular workflow.

Your estimate should size the yearly pool of relevant project-manager buyers, define what portion enters a first-time onboarding flow, and translate that into a business opportunity tied to retention. The focus is not just market sizing, but showing how better onboarding could influence activation, continued usage, renewal, expansion, or reduced early churn.

Assume the product could be a large-scale SaaS or productivity platform used by project managers to coordinate teams, tasks, timelines, stakeholders, and reporting. You should make reasonable assumptions where data is missing, clearly state them, and distinguish between user counts, buyer counts, paid accounts, and retained customers.

The experience should consider:

- The target population: professional project managers, team leads acting as project managers, and buyers responsible for adopting project-management tools.
- The unit of estimation: annual first-time buyers, paid workspaces/accounts, seats influenced, or revenue opportunity.
- Adoption and buying frequency: how often project managers evaluate or switch tools, start new projects, join new organizations, or purchase software for a team.
- Funnel assumptions: awareness, trial/signup, first purchase, onboarding completion, activation, and retention.
- Retention linkage: how onboarding quality could affect early churn, repeat usage, renewal, team adoption, or expansion.
- Segmentation: company size, geography, industry, solo vs team purchase, self-serve vs sales-assisted buying, and new vs switching customers.
- Sensitivity checks: which assumptions most affect the estimate and what high/base/low cases might look like.
- Sanity checks: comparing the estimate against plausible numbers of project managers, organizations, software buyers, and annual SaaS purchasing behavior.

Your goal is to present a structured, defensible guesstimate that sizes the annual onboarding opportunity and explains why it matters for retention, without needing exact market data.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in cost efficiency for usage-based billing console
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are investigating an incident in a usage-based billing console used by product analysts to understand metered consumption, attribute costs to products or teams, and make decisions about pricing, capacity, experiments, and customer behavior. Recently, the reported cost efficiency for this analyst segment dropped suddenly, raising concern that analysts are spending more to achieve the same analytical outcomes or that the console is surfacing a distorted view of usage and cost.

Your task is to diagnose the issue before proposing any fixes. Treat this as a root-cause analysis exercise: clarify what “cost efficiency” means in this context, determine whether the drop is real or measurement-related, identify when and where the anomaly began, and build a structured set of hypotheses across product behavior, data pipelines, billing logic, user mix, pricing changes, and operational events.

The investigation should account for the fact that usage-based billing systems often depend on event ingestion, aggregation windows, pricing rules, customer/account hierarchies, permissions, dashboards, and analyst workflows. A sudden change may come from actual usage behavior, a metering or attribution bug, a UI/reporting change, delayed data, pricing configuration, or a segment-specific shift in how product analysts use the console.

The experience should consider:
- The exact metric definition for cost efficiency, including numerator, denominator, time window, and whether it is based on billed cost, estimated cost, queries run, reports generated, active analysts, or business outcomes.
- Baseline and anomaly framing: when the drop started, magnitude, duration, seasonality, and whether it is isolated to product analysts or visible across other user segments.
- Segmentation by account type, product area, geography, analyst cohort, workspace, permission level, billing plan, query type, dashboard, and data source.
- Instrumentation and data-quality checks across event logging, metering pipelines, aggregation jobs, pricing tables, currency/tax handling, attribution rules, and dashboard refresh timing.
- Hypotheses that distinguish real cost increases from reduced analyst output, incorrect cost allocation, duplicate metering, missing usage events, changed user behavior, or a recent product/configuration release.
- Evidence needed to validate or reject hypotheses, including logs, release history, billing records, audit trails, support tickets, cohort trends, and comparisons against external systems of record.
- Immediate mitigation considerations if customers or internal teams are making decisions from incorrect cost-efficiency data, including communication, data backfills, and confidence labeling.
- Prevention mechanisms such as monitoring, anomaly alerts, metric ownership, reconciliation checks, and change-management controls for billing-related systems.

The goal is to demonstrate a rigorous diagnostic approach that narrows the problem from a broad metric drop to the most likely root cause, while protecting trust in the billing console and avoiding premature fixes before the evidence is clear.

title: How would you decide whether to prioritize search, permissions, or collaboration workflows for a Drive-style product under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints?
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a strategic prioritization decision for a Drive-style cloud file collaboration product used by student project teams. These teams create, store, share, and co-edit files across classes, clubs, research groups, and time-bound assignments, often with mixed devices, varying technical skill levels, and changing membership.

The product team must decide whether the next major investment should focus on improving search, permissions, or collaboration workflows. Each area can plausibly improve collaboration activation, but they differ in user value, technical complexity, trust implications, cost, and regulatory exposure. The decision is especially difficult because student teams need fast coordination, but also expect privacy, safe sharing, accessibility, and reliability at global scale.

This is a strategy question: you are not being asked to design the final feature. You are being asked to frame the market and product decision, compare options, identify trade-offs, and define how you would decide what to prioritize under scale, incentive, and regulatory constraints.

The experience should consider:

- The target users: student project teams, including owners, contributors, reviewers, and occasional external collaborators.
- The core workflow: finding relevant files, understanding who has access, sharing safely, collaborating in real time or asynchronously, and completing group work.
- The strategic options: search improvements, permissions simplification/control, and collaboration workflow enhancements.
- The business outcome: increasing meaningful collaboration activation, not just file uploads or storage usage.
- Trade-offs across user value, trust, technical feasibility, operational cost, accessibility, and long-term platform leverage.
- Constraints from privacy expectations, institutional policies, data quality, permission complexity, and responsible use of AI-powered capabilities.
- Decision gates such as segment impact, adoption potential, risk level, reversibility, dependency on other teams, and measurable success criteria.
- Risks including accidental oversharing, poor search relevance, fragmented collaboration behavior, regulatory non-compliance, and incentives that drive low-quality engagement.

Your goal is to explain how you would make a well-reasoned prioritization decision for Drive, showing the options you would evaluate, the evidence you would seek, the trade-offs you would weigh, and how you would determine which investment has the strongest right to win for student project teams.

title: Estimate the annual opportunity for mobile calendar assistant among restaurant owners
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating the annual business opportunity for a mobile calendar assistant designed for restaurant owners. The assistant could help owners manage reservations, supplier meetings, staff schedules, catering inquiries, private-event bookings, customer follow-ups, and reminders from a phone-first workflow.

Frame the opportunity as a guesstimate: define the relevant market, estimate how many restaurant owners or decision-makers could realistically use such a tool in a year, and translate that into a business opportunity. You should also connect the market estimate to lead conversion, such as how many prospects could become qualified leads, trials, paying customers, or booked sales conversations.

Your estimate should be grounded in clear assumptions rather than exact external data. Make the scope explicit, show the calculation structure, and identify which assumptions most influence the final opportunity size.

The experience should consider:
- The geographic scope and time period of the estimate, with “annual opportunity” clearly defined
- The unit of analysis, such as restaurant locations, owners, operators, or decision-makers
- Relevant restaurant segments, including independent restaurants, small chains, cafés, bars, and multi-location operators
- Mobile readiness and calendar-assistant fit based on owner workflow frequency and pain intensity
- Adoption assumptions, including awareness, willingness to try, and likelihood of recurring use
- Lead-conversion funnel stages, from reachable prospects to qualified leads and customers
- Sensitivity of the estimate to major assumptions such as market size, conversion rate, pricing, and retention
- Sanity checks to ensure the final number is directionally credible

Your goal is to produce a structured, defensible estimate of the annual opportunity and explain how that opportunity could translate into a lead-generation or sales funnel for a mobile calendar assistant serving restaurant owners.

title: Create a launch plan for returns management portal aimed at enterprise admins
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are launching a returns management portal for enterprise admins who oversee high-volume return workflows across orders, refunds, exchanges, warehouses, customer support, and finance operations. The portal is intended to help admins configure return policies, monitor return status, reconcile refunds, resolve exceptions, and ensure that payments tied to returns are processed accurately and on time.

The launch plan should focus specifically on execution: how to move from readiness to rollout while optimizing for payment reliability. This includes ensuring refunds, reversals, partial payments, store credits, payment-method fallbacks, and reconciliation flows work consistently across enterprise accounts, payment processors, regions, and edge cases.

Assume the product is business-critical for large customers, where payment failures can create customer escalations, accounting discrepancies, regulatory exposure, and loss of trust. Your plan should account for cross-functional coordination across product, engineering, payments, operations, finance, support, compliance, sales/customer success, and enterprise customers.

The experience should consider:

- Launch scope, including which return and payment workflows are included in the first release versus deferred
- Owners and responsibilities across product, engineering, payments, finance, operations, support, and customer-facing teams
- Dependencies on payment processors, order systems, warehouse systems, refund ledgers, accounting tools, and admin permissions
- Sequencing of alpha, beta, pilot, phased rollout, and general availability for enterprise accounts
- Go/no-go criteria tied to payment success rate, refund latency, reconciliation accuracy, error rates, and support readiness
- Rollback, failover, and incident response plans for failed refunds, duplicate payments, delayed payouts, or ledger mismatches
- Customer and internal communication plans, including admin training, support playbooks, status messaging, and escalation paths
- Launch risks such as integration gaps, regional payment differences, permission misconfiguration, reporting inaccuracies, and operational overload

Your goal is to present a clear, practical launch plan that shows how you would safely release the portal, coordinate teams, reduce payment-related risk, and ensure enterprise admins can trust the returns and refund experience from day one.

title: Tell me about leading ambiguous work related to identity verification flow
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are being asked to describe a real situation where you led ambiguous work around an identity verification flow used by clinic administrators. The scenario should involve a healthcare or healthcare-adjacent workflow where administrators need to verify their own identity, clinic affiliation, authority to manage accounts, or access to sensitive operational/patient-related systems.

Focus on how you operated when the problem was unclear: incomplete requirements, unclear ownership, regulatory or security constraints, conflicting stakeholder views, data quality issues, manual review bottlenecks, user frustration, or high-risk failure modes such as false approvals, false rejections, duplicate clinic records, or delayed access. The interviewer is looking for evidence that you could structure ambiguity, drive cross-functional alignment, and improve quality without compromising trust, compliance, or user experience.

Your story should show your role in moving the work from uncertainty to resolution. This may include how you diagnosed the issue, defined quality, partnered with design, engineering, operations, compliance, support, or risk teams, made trade-offs, and measured whether the resolution actually improved the verification experience for clinic administrators.

The experience should consider:
- The specific identity verification workflow and where clinic administrators experienced friction or risk
- What made the work ambiguous, such as unclear requirements, limited data, edge cases, or stakeholder disagreement
- Your direct ownership and how you created structure, priorities, and decision-making clarity
- How you balanced administrator experience, verification accuracy, operational effort, privacy, security, and compliance
- The quality issues you identified and the mechanisms you used to resolve them
- Cross-functional partners involved and how you aligned them around a path forward
- The measurable impact of the resolution, including user, operational, risk, or business outcomes
- What you learned and how it changed future product, process, or verification quality practices

The goal is to demonstrate a strong behavioral example of product leadership in a sensitive, high-stakes workflow: turning ambiguity into an actionable plan, improving the quality of identity verification, and earning trust from both internal teams and clinic administrators.

title: If you were building an autocomplete experience, how would you use underlying data to predict the next word a person is going to type?
description:
Context
Users seek efficient typing assistance through autocomplete features. Leveraging data improves user experience by predicting next words accurately.

Key details
- Users: Users seeking typing assistance
- Product: Autocomplete experience
- Goal: Improve prediction accuracy of next words
- Scope: Utilize historical user input and common phrases

Key terms
- n-grams: A contiguous sequence of n items from a given sample of text
- machine learning: Algorithms that improve automatically through experience and data

How you'll be evaluated
System understanding · Technical trade-offs · Scalability and reliability · Communication

title: Define success metrics for support ticket summarizer serving enterprise admins
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating a support ticket summarizer used by enterprise admins who manage high-volume customer or employee support queues. The summarizer turns long ticket threads, attachments, prior agent notes, system events, and customer history into concise summaries that help admins and support teams understand the issue, route it correctly, and drive a high-quality resolution.

The main business goal is quality resolution, not simply faster handling. In this context, “success” should capture whether summaries help teams resolve the right problem accurately, completely, and with customer trust, while avoiding hallucinations, missing context, privacy issues, or over-reliance on AI-generated content.

Your task is to define a metrics framework for evaluating this product experience. The framework should make clear what outcomes matter, how they would be measured, which users and workflows are included, and how the metrics would guide product decisions before and after launch.

The experience should consider:
- How to define “quality resolution” for enterprise support workflows, including resolution correctness, completeness, durability, and customer/admin satisfaction.
- The right denominators, such as tickets summarized, tickets viewed by admins, tickets resolved after summary use, eligible tickets, or enterprise accounts using the feature.
- Instrumentation needed to connect summary generation, admin consumption, ticket actions, escalations, reopens, SLA performance, and final resolution outcomes.
- Cohorts and segments, including ticket complexity, channel, priority, language, product area, customer tier, admin role, and new versus experienced support teams.
- Summary quality signals, including accuracy, relevance, missing critical details, hallucinated information, freshness, and usefulness in handoff or escalation.
- Guardrail metrics for responsible AI and enterprise trust, such as privacy leakage, unsafe content, compliance violations, bias across languages or regions, and admin override behavior.
- Operational and product health metrics, including latency, availability, coverage, cost per summary, adoption, repeat usage, and impact on support team workload.
- Decision usefulness, including how the metrics would indicate whether to launch, expand, tune the model, restrict use cases, or require human review.

The goal is to propose a clear, decision-oriented measurement approach that balances business impact, user value, AI quality, and enterprise risk. Your answer should show how you would know whether the summarizer is genuinely improving support outcomes rather than only making the workflow appear faster or more automated.

title: Decide whether to invest in community reporting flow for on-call engineers to improve recovery rate
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether a large-scale technology product should invest in a community reporting flow that helps on-call engineers detect, triage, and recover from incidents or user-facing issues faster. The “community” may include end users, moderators, customer support, developers, sellers, creators, or other external/internal reporters who notice problems before automated monitoring fully captures the impact.

Today, on-call engineers may receive fragmented signals from alerts, support tickets, social channels, internal escalations, and ad hoc messages. This can create noise, duplicate reports, unclear severity, missing reproduction details, and delayed ownership. The proposed investment is intended to improve recovery rate, but it may also introduce moderation burden, false positives, privacy concerns, abuse vectors, and operational complexity.

Your task is to make a clear strategic recommendation on whether to invest now, defer, run a smaller test, or pursue an alternative. Frame the decision around the size and urgency of the recovery problem, the users and workflows affected, the company’s right to win, and the trade-offs versus other reliability or incident-management investments.

The decision should consider:
- The specific recovery-rate problem being addressed, including how “recovery” is defined and where current breakdowns occur.
- Which reporting communities matter most, what they are able to observe, and how credible or actionable their reports are.
- The end-to-end on-call workflow: report intake, deduplication, severity assessment, routing, escalation, incident response, resolution, and follow-up.
- Strategic options such as building a full reporting flow, improving existing alerting/support channels, starting with a limited pilot, or not investing.
- Expected benefits across customer trust, operational leverage, incident detection speed, and reduced time to recovery.
- Key costs and risks, including engineer interruption, report quality, spam or abuse, privacy/security exposure, accessibility, and global support needs.
- Decision gates and success criteria that would justify scaling the investment or stopping it.
- Dependencies on tooling, staffing, observability systems, support operations, and incident-management processes.

The goal is to produce a structured recommendation that shows how you would evaluate the opportunity, compare alternatives, manage risks, and decide whether this investment is the right way to improve recovery rate for on-call engineering teams.

title: Estimate the annual addressable market for Alexa among enterprise cloud buyers
description:

How you'll be evaluated
Clear structure · Reasonable assumptions · Math accuracy · Sanity check

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in conversion for content recommendation feed
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are the product manager for a content recommendation feed used by on-call engineers to discover and act on relevant operational content, such as incident runbooks, alerts context, postmortems, troubleshooting guides, or recommended next steps. The feed has a defined conversion event, such as opening a recommended item, saving it, launching a workflow, or completing a recommended action. A sudden drop in conversion has been detected among on-call engineers.

Your task is to diagnose the issue before recommending fixes. Focus on how you would frame the anomaly, validate whether it is real, isolate where in the user journey the drop occurred, and form evidence-based hypotheses across product, data, ranking, user behavior, and operational factors.

This is an RCA-style interview question. You are not expected to jump to solutions immediately. The interviewer is looking for a structured investigation that distinguishes measurement issues from real user impact, narrows the affected surface area, and identifies what evidence would increase or decrease confidence in each hypothesis.

The experience should consider:
- The exact definition of “conversion,” including numerator, denominator, time window, and whether the event is tied to impressions, sessions, users, or recommendations.
- Segmentation by on-call cohort, team, geography, device, surface, alert severity, incident state, tenure, and traffic source.
- Funnel breakdown from feed exposure to recommendation impression, click/open, engagement, and final conversion.
- Instrumentation checks for logging gaps, schema changes, delayed pipelines, duplicate events, bot/internal traffic, and experiment assignment issues.
- Recent changes to ranking models, content supply, permissions, personalization, UI, notification triggers, or incident-management integrations.
- External context such as incident volume, seasonality, work schedules, paging load, or changes in engineer behavior during outages.
- Evidence needed to prioritize hypotheses, including dashboards, logs, experiment data, qualitative feedback, and comparison against unaffected segments.
- Immediate mitigation and prevention considerations once the root cause is understood, including monitoring, alerting, and ownership.

The goal is to show how you would lead a calm, rigorous diagnosis of a sudden conversion drop in a high-trust operational workflow, separating symptoms from root causes and ensuring any eventual fix is based on reliable evidence rather than assumptions.

title: Describe a time you shipped under ambiguity for small businesses in the context of creator analytics for small businesses
description:
Problem Statement Description

Describe a real situation where you shipped a product, feature, or meaningful improvement despite significant ambiguity, specifically in a creator analytics context serving small businesses. The focus is on how you operated when customer needs, data interpretation, success criteria, technical feasibility, or go-to-market assumptions were not fully clear.

Small businesses using creator analytics often need to decide which content, channels, campaigns, creators, or audiences are worth investing in, but they may lack analytics expertise, clean data, or time to interpret complex dashboards. Your example should show how you helped move from uncertainty to a shipped outcome that improved decision quality for these users.

Choose a story where you had meaningful ownership, not just participation. The interviewer is looking for how you framed ambiguity, aligned stakeholders, made trade-offs, managed risk, learned from customers or data, and measured whether the shipped work actually helped small-business users make better decisions.

The experience should consider:
- What was ambiguous at the start: customer problem, metric definition, data quality, product scope, technical feasibility, business priority, or stakeholder alignment
- Who the small-business users were and what decisions they were trying to make using creator analytics
- Your specific role, ownership, and decision-making authority
- How you gathered evidence from users, data, research, sales/support, experiments, or market signals
- The trade-offs you made between speed, confidence, usability, accuracy, and business impact
- How you aligned cross-functional partners such as engineering, design, data science, sales, marketing, or leadership
- What shipped, how success was measured, and what changed for customers or the business
- What you learned, what you would do differently, and how the experience shaped your product judgment

Your goal is to tell a concise but high-signal story that demonstrates product leadership under uncertainty: how you created clarity, shipped responsibly, improved outcomes for small-business customers, and reflected honestly on the results.

title: Debug a spike in complaints from mobile-first viewers on Creator Tools at global scale

Structured diagnosis · Hypothesis prioritization · Data validation · Fix and prevention

title: Evaluate the technical trade-offs of adding AI to appointment booking
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether and how to add AI capabilities to an appointment-booking product used by remote teams to schedule meetings, customer calls, interviews, demos, and internal sessions across time zones. The current booking flow likely involves calendar availability, invitee preferences, time-zone handling, reminders, rescheduling, and integrations with tools such as calendars, video conferencing, CRM, or messaging platforms.

The interview focuses on the technical product trade-offs behind introducing AI into this workflow, not simply on brainstorming AI features. You should frame what AI might help with, where deterministic scheduling logic may be safer, what data and integrations are required, and how the system should preserve trust when dealing with calendars, availability, personal information, and business-critical meetings.

Consider the needs of remote teams that value speed, accuracy, transparency, and low coordination overhead. AI may create leverage by reducing back-and-forth, interpreting natural language requests, recommending optimal slots, handling exceptions, or improving follow-ups, but it may also introduce latency, cost, ambiguity, privacy risk, hallucinations, and user-control concerns.

The experience should consider:
- Core user workflows, including creating bookings, finding availability, handling time zones, rescheduling, cancellations, reminders, and multi-party coordination.
- Technical requirements for calendar APIs, identity, permissions, availability data, event metadata, conferencing links, notifications, and third-party integrations.
- AI-specific trade-offs around model accuracy, explainability, confidence thresholds, fallback behavior, question/data design, latency, cost, and deterministic versus probabilistic decision-making.
- Reliability expectations for successful bookings, including duplicate prevention, race conditions, calendar sync delays, offline states, and failure recovery.
- Privacy, security, and compliance considerations for calendar content, attendee data, sensitive meeting titles, enterprise controls, data retention, and consent.
- Rollout strategy across user segments, such as individual users, small remote teams, enterprise admins, external invitees, and high-volume scheduling use cases.
- Observability and measurement needs, including booking success, manual intervention, AI correction rate, latency, user overrides, failed bookings, and support escalations.
- Product trade-offs between automation and user control, simplicity and configurability, personalization and privacy, and short-term convenience versus long-term trust.

Your goal is to evaluate the technical feasibility, risks, and product implications of adding AI to appointment booking in a way that improves successful bookings for remote teams while maintaining reliability, user trust, and operational scalability.

title: Decide whether to invest in voice note capture for community managers to improve recommendation relevance
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are evaluating whether a large-scale community platform should invest in voice note capture for community managers as a way to improve recommendation relevance. Community managers interact with members, observe emerging needs, moderate discussions, run events, and often capture qualitative context that may not appear cleanly in structured product signals. The question is whether enabling them to record quick voice notes can create enough incremental insight to improve recommendations for content, groups, experts, events, or member connections.

Today, this workflow may rely on manual tagging, written notes, CRM-style fields, chat summaries, or informal memory. Voice capture could reduce friction for busy community managers and preserve richer context, but it also introduces questions around transcription quality, privacy, consent, operational review, model integration, and whether unstructured notes can reliably improve recommendation outcomes at scale.

Your task is to make a clear strategic recommendation on whether to invest, defer, pilot, or avoid this capability. Frame the market and product opportunity, compare plausible alternatives, and identify the trade-offs and decision gates that would determine whether this is a high-leverage investment.

The experience should consider:
- The primary users: community managers capturing observations during or after member interactions, events, moderation moments, or community health reviews.
- The intended business outcome: measurably better recommendation relevance, not just easier note-taking.
- Alternative approaches, such as better structured tagging, automated summarization of existing conversations, surveys, behavioral signals, or improved recommendation models.
- The platform’s right to win: access to unique community context, trusted manager-member relationships, and ability to connect qualitative input to recommendation systems.
- Key risks, including privacy, consent, sensitive member information, transcription errors, bias in manager observations, and operational overhead.
- Trade-offs between speed of capture, data quality, trust, cost, and scalability across different communities, languages, and manager workflows.
- Decision gates for investment, such as evidence of unmet workflow need, expected lift in recommendation quality, adoption by managers, data usability, and compliance readiness.

The goal is to present a structured recommendation that shows whether voice note capture is strategically worthwhile, what evidence would be needed to proceed, and how the team should think about investment priority relative to other ways of improving recommendation relevance.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in admin confidence for customer feedback hub
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are investigating a sudden drop in “admin confidence” among content moderators who use a customer feedback hub to review, classify, escalate, and act on customer-reported issues. The hub likely aggregates feedback from multiple sources, surfaces queues or trends, supports moderation decisions, and may include AI-assisted summaries, prioritization, routing, or policy guidance.

The drop is recent and unexpected, so your task is to frame the anomaly before recommending any fixes. Focus on understanding what “admin confidence” means in this workflow, whether the decline reflects a real product or operational issue, and which users, queues, content types, geographies, policies, or system changes are most affected.

Assume moderators depend on the hub to make accurate, timely, and defensible decisions at scale. A confidence drop could affect queue throughput, escalation quality, customer trust, policy enforcement consistency, and moderator willingness to rely on the tool.

The experience should consider:
- How “admin confidence” is defined, measured, and interpreted, including survey scores, override rates, escalation rates, decision reversals, or qualitative feedback.
- Whether the drop is broad-based or isolated by moderator cohort, tenure, region, language, queue type, feedback source, policy area, platform, or workflow step.
- Instrumentation checks to confirm the metric is accurate, comparable over time, and not affected by logging, sampling, survey exposure, denominator, or dashboard changes.
- Recent product, model, policy, tooling, data pipeline, staffing, or operational changes that could plausibly affect moderator trust in the hub.
- Hypotheses around user-facing friction, such as unclear recommendations, stale customer context, incorrect prioritization, slow load times, missing evidence, confusing UI changes, or inconsistent policy guidance.
- Evidence needed to validate or reject hypotheses, including behavioral data, moderator interviews, audit outcomes, quality reviews, incident logs, and support tickets.
- Mitigation paths if the issue is actively harming moderation quality or customer outcomes, while avoiding premature fixes before root cause is established.
- Prevention mechanisms such as monitoring, alerting, experiment guardrails, launch reviews, and feedback loops for moderator-facing changes.

Your goal is to present a structured RCA approach that narrows the problem from a vague confidence decline to a well-evidenced root cause or set of likely causes, with clear next steps for containment, validation, and longer-term prevention.

title: Diagnose a sudden drop in customer satisfaction for low-bandwidth collaboration mode
description:
Problem Statement Description

You are investigating a sudden drop in customer satisfaction tied to support agents using a low-bandwidth collaboration mode. This mode is intended to help agents continue working with customers and teammates when network conditions are poor, such as during screen sharing, internal escalation, co-browsing, chat handoff, or lightweight voice/video collaboration.

The issue is recent and appears concentrated among support workflows that rely on this mode. Before recommending fixes, your task is to structure a root-cause analysis that separates a real customer-impacting problem from measurement noise, identifies where in the agent/customer workflow the degradation is happening, and determines whether the cause is product, infrastructure, operational, or behavioral.

You should assume this is a live production environment with global users, varied network quality, multiple support channels, and high sensitivity to customer trust. The diagnosis should be practical enough to guide engineering, support operations, and product teams toward the right next steps.

The experience should consider:
- How to define the anomaly: CSAT metric, baseline, time window, affected geographies, support queues, customer types, and agent cohorts.
- Whether the drop is isolated to low-bandwidth collaboration mode or also visible in normal-bandwidth sessions, non-collaboration workflows, or specific support channels.
- Instrumentation checks, including CSAT collection changes, missing events, survey response bias, session tagging accuracy, and recent analytics pipeline changes.
- Funnel and workflow segmentation, such as session start, connection degradation, fallback activation, escalation, handoff, resolution, and post-interaction survey completion.
- Product and technical hypotheses, including latency, dropped connections, degraded audio/video/chat quality, sync issues, permission failures, UI confusion, or unexpected mode activation.
- Operational hypotheses, such as new agent training, staffing changes, queue mix shifts, policy updates, scripted responses, or higher-severity customer issues.
- Evidence needed to prioritize causes, including logs, session quality metrics, agent feedback, customer verbatims, release timelines, incident reports, and comparative cohorts.
- Immediate containment, communication, and prevention considerations without jumping prematurely to a permanent fix.

The goal is to demonstrate how you would lead a disciplined RCA: validate the signal, narrow the blast radius, generate and test hypotheses, identify the most likely root cause, and define what evidence would be required before moving into remediation.
